In a recent development, "Jaewon has been instrumental in turning the vision for Risant Health into reality," said Greg Adams, chair and chief executive officer of Kaiser Permanente and chair of the board of Risant Health. "He built an exceptional leadership team, established the organization's operating model, and positioned Risant Health to help more communities benefit from value-based care.”.

In a recent development, ryu served as Risant Health’s inaugural CEO, establishing its operating model and recruiting the initial leadership team. Key moments in his tenure include the addition of both Geisinger and Cone Health as well as meaningful clinical and operational improvements.

The interim CEO, Dale Maxwell, brings over 24 years of executive leadership experience at Presbyterian Healthcare Services, Upcoming Mexico's largest nonprofit integrated health system.

"This leadership transition reflects thoughtful planning, not a change in strategy," Adams stated. "Kaiser Permanente and Risant Health will continue to advance their mission to help leading community-based health systems deliver high-quality, value-based care. We are confident in the organization's leadership, its momentum, and its future.".

>Paul Smith and Frederick Crawford were elected as new members of the Humana board, effective immediately.

Smith currently serves as the chief commercial officer at Anthropic, PBC, leading commercial strategy and go-to-market operations. Prior to joining Anthropic, he was chief commercial officer and president of global customer and field operations at ServiceNow and held senior leadership roles at Salesforce and Microsoft.

Industry observers note that crawford also brings significant experience to the Humana board, having spent more than 30 years in the insurance and banking industries. Before his retirement in 2024, Crawford was president and chief operating officer at Aflac. He also sits on the Board of Webster Financial Corporation as a member of both the Audit and Risk committees.

In a recent development, “We are pleased to welcome Paul and Fred to the Humana Board. Paul has deep experience guiding the world’s largest enterprises in responsibly adopting technology and AI at scale along with a strong track record in product development and client service, while Fred brings broad industry experience and financial expertise focused on disciplined capital allocation and risk management,” stated Humana Chairman of the Board Kurt J. Hilzinger.

>Centene announced that Kenneth A. Burdick has retired from the manufacturer's board of directors, effective July 28, and that Paul J. Diaz has been appointed to the board, effective immediately.

Burdick joined the Centene board of directors in January 2022, offering insight that drew upon his long-standing leadership in healthcare. He served as executive vice president of products and markets at Centene and before that was the chief executive officer of WellCare Health Looks.

According to recent reports, diaz is right now a managing partner at Cressey & Manufacturer, a private investment firm focused on cultivating high-quality healthcare firms. Before joining Cressey, he was president and CEO of Myriad Genetics Inc., as well as CEO of Kindred Healthcare. He has also served on the board of healthcare organizations, such as DaVita and PharMerica.

Sources indicate that "Ken has been a valued member of our Board. His deep industry expertise, strategic perspective, and commitment to improving healthcare have made a meaningful impact on Centene. On behalf of the Board, we thank him for his service and wish him all the best in retirement," noted Frederick H. Eppinger, Chair of Centene's Board of Directors. "We are also pleased to welcome Paul Diaz to the Board. His extensive healthcare leadership experience, public tech giant governance expertise and record of guiding organizations through growth and transformation will bring valuable perspective as Centene continues to advance its strategy and serve its members.".

In a recent development, >Siemens Healthineers announced on July 30 that João Seabra will succeed John Kowal as president and head of the Americas for Siemens Healthineers, effective Oct. 1, 2026. He is at the moment the head of Siemens Healthineers Enterprise Services.

Sources indicate that seabra joined Healthineers in 2001, and from 2015 to 2018, he led the Western Europe and West Africa regions. In his most recent role as head of enterprise services, he quadrupled its revenue over the last eight years.

“We would like to thank John for his many years of successful service and outstanding commitment to Siemens Healthineers, first within our Varian business and later as President and Head of our Americas business. We are very pleased to appoint João Seabra as our new President and Head of the Americas. Under his leadership and thanks to his innovative thinking, Siemens Healthineers paved the way in our industry by creating Value Partnerships of increasing scope and impact with key customers,” said Darleen Caron, Member of the Managing Board at Siemens Healthineers with responsibility for the Americas and Chief Human Resources Officer.

>PayZen, an AI-driven patient affordability platform, has confirmed that Jingwei Wu will serve as senior vice president of engineering.

Prior to joining PayZen, Wu led the engineering team behind the LinkedIn Jobs Marketplace, expanding it to reach millions more job searchers. He’s also been part of engineering leadership teams at both Twitter and Tinder.

In his new role at PayZen, Wu will lead the manufacturer’s engineering organization, overseeing platform architecture, AI infrastructure and product engineering.

“Healthcare affordability is one of the biggest challenges facing patients and providers today, and PayZen is proving that AI can fundamentally improve how people access and pay for care,” Wu said.

>Sarah Bast was appointed as the chief marketing officer of OptimizeRx, a healthcare technology solutions provider.

According to recent reports, she brings over two decades of experience from companies including Publicis Health Media, Lilly, Bayer, Johnson & Johnson and AstraZeneca. In these roles, she developed significant expertise in point of care media strategy, which she will bring to her role at OptimizeRX.

As CMO, Bast will lead Optimize Rx’s marketing strategy and continue strengthening the organization's relationships with healthcare marketing agencies.

It has been revealed that "Sarah's decision to join OptimizeRx speaks to both the strength of the business we've built and the tremendous opportunity ahead," noted Steve Silvestro, Chief Executive Officer, OptimizeRx. "She has spent her career helping life sciences brands solve complex marketing challenges and understands firsthand how healthcare marketers can reach providers more effectively. As OptimizeRx enters its next phase of growth, her strategic vision and deep understanding of the market will help us strengthen our customer relationships and accelerate the development of solutions that improve healthcare engagement.".

According to recent reports, >Matt Swafford has been named executive vice president and chief financial officer of Peace Health, succeeding Ric Magnuson, the current interim CFO. He will join the organization on September 21 from St. Charles Health System, where he currently serves as CFO and senior VP of strategy and finance.

Swafford brings over 35 years of experience in nonprofit health system finance, helping health systems navigate change and invest in patients.

Sarah Ness, PeaceHealth president and chief executive officer, said, “We are creating a stronger PeaceHealth, one that is easier for patients to navigate, better connected for caregivers and positioned to meet the needs of our communities well into the future. Matt has shared with me that he sees every financial decision through that human lens, which makes him a strong fit for our Mission and our commitment to put people first.”.

>Hannah Alphs Jackson, M.D. will join Availity, the nation’s largest real-time health information network, as the company's first chief medical officer.

Availity remarked in a statement that it created the CMO role “to ensure clinical expertise is injected throughout the organization's strategy, innovation, and customer solutions.” This is significant as the healthcare industry and Availity continues to become dependent on automation and AI, executives said.

Before joining Availity, Alphs Jackson held roles in physician and payer leadership, where she integrated value-based care models with clinical operations. In her upcoming role as CMO, she will guide the responsible usage of emerging technologies, as part of Availity’s clinical strategy.

Recent findings suggest that “Dr. Jackson brings a rare combination of clinical expertise, provider perspective, payer experience and strategic vision,” said Russ Thomas, CEO of Availity, in a statement. “As healthcare continues to evolve, it's critical that we have strong clinical leadership guiding how we integrate automation and AI capabilities to support the entire healthcare system – and ultimately improve the entire experience.”.

>Clinical AI assistant startup Nabla declared the appointment of Brian Manning as its latest CEO to lead the manufacturer's next phase of growth.

Manning joins Nabla from Bamboo Health, where he served as president and chief revenue officer and helped scale the tech giant to more than $140 million in revenue. He also assisted in the growth and development of PatientPing and Zocdoc.

According to recent reports, as Nabla continues to expand, supporting more than 190 healthcare organizations and 100,000 clinicians, Manning will spearhead the company’s scaling efforts. His more than 20 years of experience accelerating growth will ensure that Nabla continues to be adopted across the healthcare industry, executives said in a press release.

"Healthcare organizations are looking for partners that can deliver real value today while helping them prepare for the future of AI. Nabla has built an exceptional foundation and has earned the trust of clinicians and healthcare organizations. The opportunity now is to accelerate that momentum, expand our reach, and further establish Nabla as the clinical AI partner of choice for healthcare organizations across the world,” noted Manning.

>Aptarro, a company that provides healthcare revenue cycle management software solutions, hired Paul Wiley as chief growth officer.

Wiley’s appointment comes at a significant time for Aptarro as the company continue to scale its engine for denial prevention and reimbursement intelligence. Wiley has more than two decades of executive leadership experience spanning healthcare technology, enterprise software, AI and travel technology, according to the company, and he has been tapped to steer the company through its current commercial growth.

Recent findings suggest that most recently, he served as chief commercial officer at Avodah, and prior to that, he founded Opargo, an AI-powered healthcare scheduling company. His experience will ensure that Aptarro continues to effectively address the persistent and costly problem of denials, executives said.

"As reimbursement continues to grow more dynamic, healthcare organizations need technology that evolves alongside it. We're building the leadership team to support that mission," mentioned Jeff Diamond, Aptarro CEO. "Paul's experience will be instrumental as we continue expanding our platform and defining the future of reimbursement intelligence.".

>The Pharmaceutical Care Management Association (PCMA) added two senior public affairs leaders to its team. Mackay Jimeson will join PCMA as Vice President of Coalitions, and Christine Rex will join as Senior Director of State Communications.

Jimeson joins PCMA from Patients Rising, where he was served as Executive Director, expanding the organization’s national influence and strengthening its role in health care policy. In his upcoming role at PCMA, he will lead PCMA’s coalition strategy and third-party partnership engagement efforts.

Rex will oversee state campaigns and coalition communications, while working closely with PCMA's member companies.

It has been revealed that “Bringing this level of talent reflects PCMA’s commitment to strategically meeting the needs of this moment,” stated David Marin, President and CEO of PCMA. “The pharmacy benefit manager industry has been transformed and is more responsive than ever, and we are entering a fresh era of advocacy at PCMA. MacKay will use his unique experience advocating for patients to strengthen our coalition partnerships and build broader alliances for the industry and the 289 million patients we serve. Christine is a battle-tested communicator who expertly navigates state legislative debates. Our team is deeper and more dynamic having them at PCMA.”.

Recent findings suggest that >Vanderbilt Health has chosen David C. Miller as the successor to Jeff Balser as President and CEO and Dean of Vanderbilt University School of Medicine.

Recent findings suggest that miller is presently serving as Chief Executive Officer of Michigan Medicine and Executive Vice President for Medical Affairs for the University of Michigan and will assume the role at Vanderbilt on January 1, 2027. Earlie this year, Balser unveiled plans to retire on December 31, after serving Vanderbilt in leadership roles for nearly two decades.

It has been revealed that miller’s experience at the similarly sized Michigan Health uniquely prepares him to become Vanderbilt Health’s fresh leader, the health system said. Miller’s selection as the new senior leader for Vanderbilt Health and Vanderbilt University School of Medicine finalizes an extensive national search by the VH Board of Directors to identify Balser’s successor.

As Chief Executive Officer, Miller will be responsible for shaping the future strategic direction of Vanderbilt Health and maintaining the scholarly activities shared by the Medical Center and University.

“From an incredibly strong field of applicants, Dr. Miller’s personal warmth, prior leadership experiences, and commitment to organizational culture stood out. David has presented an exciting vision for advancing the Medical Center’s missions and is the ideal candidate to succeed Dr. Balser. We look forward to welcoming David, his wife, Inge, and family to the Nashville community,” said Edie Carell Johnson, Chair of the VH Board of Directors.

According to recent reports, >Aledade appointed Darren Thayne as chief technology officer and hired Josh C. Mandel, M.D. as chief scientist. Thayne and Mandel will bring deep expertise in enterprise scale and open data standards to the firm, Aledade remarked.

Leveraging their combined experience, Aledade will further integrate advanced AI into its platform.

Recent findings suggest that thayne joins Aledade from Domo, where he spent 15 years leading its technology team, as founding technology leader, chief technology officer and executive vice president of product. He was responsible for breakthrough technology and deployment of AI-based tools that were central to customer experience.

Sources indicate that dr. Mandel, who is both a physician and software engineer, joins Aledade from Microsoft research, where he helped build open standards such as FHIR (Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources). His work will focus on external interoperability and data exchange efforts, as well as AI strategy.

“AI raises the stakes on that alignment. Deployed inside fee-for-service, it accelerates billing. Deployed inside our value-based care model, it accelerates health. Daren and Josh have built infrastructure and open standards at national scale, and they're joining us to make sure that the value created by AI in healthcare flows to patients and practices,” noted Farzad Mostashari, M.D., co-founder and CEO of Aledade.

Sources indicate that >Rad AI declared that Leonard Law will join the firm as Chief Product Officer. Law's hiring comes at a pivotal moment for the radiology reporting market, as health systems and radiology practices shift from legacy reporting software to AI-native radiology workflow platforms, the company said.

Recent findings suggest that law joins Rad AI from Primer, an enterprise AI platform, where he served as chief product officer. Previously, he was head of product at Coinbase and he also spent nearly a decade at Google Cloud and YouTube.

His appointment builds on other recent executive additions and launches, including Rad AI's next-generation speech recognition technology and appointment of David Leonard as COO. Law will work closely with Jeff Chang, M.D., co-founder and president of Rad AI, to build on the firm’s radiologist-led product foundation and help scale the next generation of AI-native workflow solutions.

Recent findings suggest that >Laura Kaiser, the president and CEO of SSM Health, has been elected by the American Hospital Association (AHA) Board of Trustees as its chair-elect designate. She will serve as chair-elect in 2027, eventually becoming chair of AHA and the top elected official of the national organization that represents America’s hospitals.

It has been revealed that since 2017, Kaiser has been a crucial part of SSM Health, which serves serves millions of patients across Missouri, Illinois, Wisconsin and Oklahoma. As part of her work with SSM Health, she transformed the health system's telehealth capabilities and announced a partnership with Siemens Healthineers to expand access to care and train healthcare workers.

She also serves on several other boards, including Greater St. Louis Inc., Merit Medical and Navitus Health Solutions.

Industry observers note that “I look forward to the opportunity to serve, continuing to advocate for America's hospitals and health systems to advance solutions that work for everyone. The AHA's vision of a society of healthy communities, where every person has the potential to live a healthy life, is one I have pursued throughout my career,” Kaiser remarked in the announcement.

>Ted Holden was named as the Vice President of Client Success for Collective Health, an independent third-party administrator that combines administration, cost management and care.

Recent findings suggest that prior to this appointment, he served as Head of Strategic Partnerships and Network Strategy at Noom and Chief Growth Officer at Catapult Health. During his early career, he spent over 20 years at BlueCross BlueShield of Texas.

Holden will lead a team delivering a stellar experience to Collective Health’s self-funded employer clients, drawing on his relationships across the healthcare industry and his robust experience, the firm mentioned.

“I’ve spent my career on the carrier side, the digital health side, and everywhere in between, and what Collective Health has built is genuinely different,” Holden mentioned in a statement. “One unified foundation that brings together administration, cost management, and care navigation, with incentives aligned with employers. I’m excited to help our clients understand what’s possible and make sure they’re getting every ounce of value from it.”.

Industry observers note that >Brian S. Kim, M.D. has been named the first vice president and chief biotechnology officer at Northwell Health, as well as head of intellectual asset management at the Feinstein Institutes. He will also join the department of dermatology as a professor at Northwell Health.

The Feinstein Institutes is home to Northwell Health’s research center, and it serves as the largest health care provider and private employer in New York State. Kim joins Feinstein from the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, bringing his expertise in dermatology, medical research and biotechnology.

His work has led to significant clinical advances, including the design of pivotal clinical trials that resulted in two first-in-class U.S. Food and Drug Administration-approved treatments for atopic dermatitis and prurigo nodularis. He has founded three biotech companies, including Alys Pharmaceuticals, and authored over 190 peer-reviewed publications.

Kim will continue to advance Feinstein Institute’s groundbreaking research on electric stimulation to treat disease, including work on nerve stimulation implants that could potentially treat Crohn’s disease and other inflammatory conditions.

Recent findings suggest that “Dr. Kim’s appointment reflects our commitment to transforming bold research into better outcomes for our patients,” noted John D’Angelo, M.D., Northwell’s president and CEO. “With his leadership, we can better translate breakthrough science and pioneer the future of medicine while staying grounded in our mission to produce knowledge to cure disease.”.

Recent findings suggest that >Anita Girard, R.N., of the American Nurses Association\California, was elected by representatives of the American Nurses Association (ANA) as the new president representing the interests of more than 5 million nurses. Her two-year term of service will begin on January 1, 2027.

Girard, a Doctor of Nursing Practice (DNP), will lead ANA’s implementation of the organization's 2026-2030 strategic strategy, and its Board of Directors. She presently serves as vice president of the American Nurses Association and most recently served as the president of the American Nurses Association\California. Prior to leading these associations, she was chief nursing officer and VP of nursing at Cedars-Sinai Medical Center in Los Angeles, California.

“I am deeply honored to be elected to serve as the next president of the American Nurses Association and to help lead this organization into its next chapter,” Girard remarked in a statement. “For more than 30 years, I have served this profession across clinical, operational, executive, and association leadership roles, and that experience has reinforced one enduring belief: nurses must be supported, respected, and empowered in every setting where they are educated and practice.”.

Sources indicate that >The University of Oklahoma’s academic health system (OU Health) has named Jonathan W. Curtright as the fresh president and CEO, effective July 1, 2026. Richard P. Lofgren, M.D., OU Health’s inaugural president and CEO, announced his retirement earlier this year and Curtright will be his replacement.

Recent findings suggest that curtright has been chief operating officer of OU Health since August 22, and under his leadership, the system saw an annual revenue increase from $1.9 billion to a projected $3.7 billion in fiscal year 2026. Admissions also increased 22.3% percent and outpatient clinic visits statewide reached more than 1 million, reflecting higher patient volumes and service intensity as opposed to acquisitions.

He was also responsible for program expansions, including investments in pediatric health, cancer centers and neonatal intensive care.

OU Health board of directors Chair G. Rainey Williams Jr. said, “Jonathan has been instrumental in helping advance OU Health’s mission and strategic vision during a period of extraordinary growth. He understands the unique responsibilities of an academic health system and has demonstrated the leadership, operational expertise and long-term vision needed to guide OU Health into its next chapter. The board is confident in his ability to build upon the strong foundation established under Dr. Lofgren’s leadership.”.

>Christopher O’Connor, the CEO of Yale New Haven Health System (YNHHS), will be leaving after 14 years with the organization.

Recent findings suggest that he will serve as a special advisor to the chair of the Board of Trustees during the transition, and the board will also be conducting a CEO search over the next months. Pamela Sutton-Wallace, the current president of YNHHS, will serve as acting CEO, effective immediately.

O’Connor joined YNHHS after leading the acquisition of the Hospital of Saint Raphael, and during his time with Yale, he oversaw multiple hospital integrations and strategic collaboration with Yale Medicine. YNHHS has been well positioned by O’Connor to open the Adams Neurosciences Center in 2027, which is the largest strategic project in the history of the academic health system, according to the release.

“We are extremely grateful to Chris for his commitment to the System and many years of service,” mentioned Mary Farrell, chair of the YNHHS Board of Trustees. “He has worked tirelessly to serve our patients and communities during the pandemic with exemplary care and results, and leaves YNHHS in a strong and successful position as we continue to offer the very best care to every one of our patients.”.

>The Medical University of South Carolina (MUSC) unveiled that their president, David J. Cole, will retire in June 2027 after 13 years. He initially joined MUSC in 1994, and Cole will remain a professor and surgical oncologist with the system.

An extensive nationwide search for Cole’s successor will be led by former board chairman and sitting trustee James Lemon, D.M.D, and conclude next spring.

During his tenure, he secured support for the construction and opening of Shawn Jenkins Children’s Hospital and Pearl Tourville Women’s Pavilion, as well as the Jean and Hugh K. Leatherman Behavioral Care Pavilion in Florence. Cole also maintained MUSC’s U.S. News & World Report accolade as the “Best Hospital” in South Carolina.

"To have had the opportunity to lead and serve this remarkable institution has been one of the great privileges of my life," Cole remarked in a statement. "MUSC stands today as one of the nation’s leading academic medical centers, a testament to what can be achieved when people are united in service to patients, students, families, communities and one another.”.

>Alice Rigdon of Mayo Clinic in Florida will join Deaconess Health System as senior vice president and chief financial officer, effective this fall. She will succeed Cheryl Wathen, who is retiring after more than 36 years with Deaconess, including 16 years as the system's CFO.

Sources indicate that at Mayo Clinic Florida, Rigdon drove capital and finance transformation initiatives, including standardization, automation and workforce development. Prior to joining Mayo Clinic, she served as VP of finance at SCL Health's Saint Joseph Hospital in Denver and as director of outpatient strategy and development and CFO of Piedmont Medical Center in South Carolina.

Wathen was initially named senior vice president and CFO of Deaconess in 2010, after serving as manager of internal audit, manager of finance, CFO of The Women's Hospital and controller of Deaconess Health System.

"What I am most proud of is the people I have hired and mentored who have excelled in their roles and will be the leaders that take Deaconess into the future,” Wathen mentioned in a statement.

Recent findings suggest that >The American Hospital Association named Steve Walsh as its upcoming president and CEO, taking over for the retiring Rick Pollack. Walsh comes from a similar role at the Massachusetts Hospital Association, and will stay there until the appointment takes effect this fall. Read more here.

>Symplr, a provider of enterprise healthcare operations software, appointed Andrew Langford as Chief Financial Officer, effective immediately. As symplr continues to scale its investment in AI-powered innovation, Langford is poised to help drive the company’s next phase of value creation and operational excellence, the company remarked. He succeeds Tom Fink, who has served as interim CFO since early 2026, and will ensure a smooth leadership transition.

It has been revealed that langford was previously an executive vice president at Zelis, where he oversaw financial strategy, treasury, enterprise pricing and operational planning for the healthcare and financial technology tech giant. Prior to Zelis, he spent nearly a decade at Global Payments, Inc. in a series of progressively senior finance leadership roles.

According to recent reports, “Andrew brings the strategic perspective, financial discipline and operational acumen that will help guide symplr through its next phase of growth,” stated Venkat Kavarthapu, symplr CEO, in a statement. “His expertise in scaling global organizations, executing strategic transactions and partnering across the business will be instrumental as we continue to invest in AI-powered innovations that reduce complexity, enhance care quality and deliver value for our customers.”.

>President Donald Trump declared on his social media platform, Truth Social, that Chris Klomp has been tapped to serve as Deputy Secretary for the Department of Health and Human Services.

Klomp, who heads the Department of Medicare at the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, has made a rapid rise through the agency to a potential role as its second-in-command. The Deputy Secretary post has been vacant since February, when Jim O'Neill departed the agency. At the same time, Klomp was elevated to a senior adviser to HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr.

In the Truth Social post, Trump remarked that Klomp's career trajectory "proves that he is a potential STAR." He said that he, Kennedy and CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz, M.D., chose Klomp as a nominee "together.".

"Chris is a Strong and Inspiring Leader and a Highly Successful Entrepreneur," Trump wrote in the post. "Everywhere Chris goes, he earns TRUST. He is a person of principle, and is deeply committed to serving the AMERICAN People — and fixing our broken Healthcare System.".

In a recent development, >Michael Wagner, MD, the President and Chief Executive Officer of Care Newly introduced England Health System (CNE), will step down as CEO and transition to become Chair of the Board of Directors. The Board has begun the process to search for CNE’s new CEO and President, aiming to have new leadership by early 2027.

Recent findings suggest that dr. Wagner joined Care New England in 2022, and he was responsible for implementing an Epic electronic health record program and a strategic planning initiative. Wagner also secured $100 million in capital in order to expand the system and restored the organization to positive operating performance. He intends to remain President and CEO until the successor has been selected and onboarded, which will ensure a smooth transition.

Gary Furtado, the current Chair of the CNE board, will continue to serve in his role until the transition is complete. Furtado mentioned in their release that: “Mike’s leadership has been transformative for Care Fresh England. His vision, commitment, and steady leadership have strengthened the organization clinically, strategically, and financially. The Board is grateful for his service as CEO and pleased that he will continue to support the organization as Board Chair.”.

>Rush University System for Health and Rush University Medical Center unveiled today that Omar Lateef, D.O., president and CEO, intends to retire from his role in June 2027. The Rush Board of Directors also announced that it will begin a national search for the next system leader in early fall.

Lateef has been connected to Rush for over 25 years, completing his fellowship training in Pulmonary and Critical Care Medicine at Rush University Medical Center in 2005 and joining the faculty afterwards. In 2019, he became the chief of pulmonary and critical care medicine, and in 2022, he became the CEO of the system.

Industry observers note that in these leadership positions, Lateef led Rush’s response to the COVID-19 pandemic, earning both him and the system widespread recognition. Under Lateef’s leadership, Rush University Medical Center’s standing among the nation’s premier academic medical centers has grown significantly, including repeated placement on the U.S. News & World Report Honor Roll, according to the organization. He helped establish national benchmarks for quality and safety through Rush’s leadership in Vizient quality outcomes.

“Omar’s career at Rush exemplifies extraordinary dedication to our mission and our patients,” said William Downe, Chair of the Rush University System for Health Board of Directors. “From his arrival as a fellow more than two decades ago to his service as President and CEO, he has helped shape Rush into the organization it is today.”.

>Madeline Bell, the CEO of Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia (CHOP), will retire on October 1, 2026, after almost 40 years with the organization. CHOP's current president, Joseph (Joe) Mitchell, M.D., will succeed her.

It has been revealed that bell, who has served as CEO for 11 years, revealed her intent to retire in 2024, beginning the search for CHOP’s new leader. In April 2025, Mitchell joined CHOP and began to work closely alongside Bell, the Board, and their C-suite to ensure a smooth transition.

Mitchell brings over 20 years of healthcare leadership experience, including roles at both Boston Children’s Hospital and Franciscan Children’s Hospital. At Franciscan, he secured approvals and capital to support its 10-year institutional master blueprint. Prior to this, he worked at McKinsey & Tech giant for 14 years, including seven years as partner.

It has been revealed that “Joe brings a fresh perspective, a patient-first approach and a strong strategic mindset," Greg Davis, chairman of CHOP’s board, stated in the announcement. "We are confident he will guide CHOP into its next chapter with continued excellence and impact.”.

>Kevin Leahy, the CEO of nonprofit Catholic healthcare ministry Franciscan Alliance, will step down from his position on December 31.

In a recent development, he plans to stay with Franciscan as an internal consultant until the end of 2027, to facilitate the leadership transition. Following this, he will retire after 48 years of service at Franciscan.

"It is our responsibility to continue Christ’s ministry in our Franciscan tradition by serving the needs of all who seek healing of body, mind and spirit, especially the most vulnerable among us," Leahy said in a statement.

In a recent development, >MultiCare Health System unveiled its CEO, William (Bill) Robertson, will retire on Dec. 31. The current president, Florence Chang, will become the health system's upcoming President and CEO beginning on Jan.1 2027.

Chang and Robertson will continue to work closely together this year to ensure a smooth transition.

Sources indicate that robertson has been part of the MultiCare team since 2014, serving as CEO since 2022 and growing MultiCare to become the largest community-based nonprofit health system in the region. He was largely responsible for their expansion across Washington state, creating a comprehensive and clinically integrated system there.

Chang joined MultiCare in 2006 as senior vice president and chief information officer. She has won multiple accolades for MultiCare, including the HIMSS Davies Organizational Award of Excellence. As executive vice president and chief operating officer, she was responsible for the smooth operation of eight hospitals and over 180 clinics.

It has been revealed that “On behalf of the Board of Directors, I want to thank Bill Robertson for his extraordinary leadership and the lasting impact he has had on MultiCare,” said John Wiborg, board chair for MultiCare Health System, in the announcement. “As MultiCare moves forward into this next chapter, the board has full confidence and trust in Florence Chang as she steps into this leadership role. She is a highly effective servant leader with a great passion for MultiCare’s mission, as well as a deep knowledge of the organization’s capabilities and areas of opportunity.”.

>Komodo Health changed its leadership structure as part of the manufacturer's long-term vision for enterprise-wide adoption of AI. Miles Ennis, former chief operating officer, has been appointed as president, while co-founder, Web Sun, will assume the role of co-CEO. They will both work alongside co-founder and CEO Arif Nathoo, M.D.

Industry observers note that ennis initially joined Komodo Health as chief revenue officer in 2024, leading one of the strongest growth periods in company history and accelerating the adoption of Marmot, which is an AI-native platform that builds evidence sets for complex questions, according to the company. In his new role as President, he will continue to scale Komodo's growth opportunities, while aligning innovation with industry needs and strengthening the company’s execution.

Industry observers note that in the firm's recent press release, both Sun and Nathoo emphasize that healthcare is moving in the direction of full AI adoption, as opposed to the previous phase of AI experimentation. Sun further states that “Miles has consistently demonstrated the ability to connect strategy, product innovation, customer needs, and execution, a capability that becomes even more notable as AI reshapes what is possible in healthcare and Life Sciences.".

>Jamie Sharp, M.D. and Chris Rigg have joined Strive Health's executive team. The value-based kidney care tech giant tapped Sharp as its newly introduced chief medical officer and Rigg joined as chief financial officer. Sharp will oversee the clinical strategy, while Rigg will assist with scaling the business and deploying new AI technologies.

Sharp previously served as chief medical officer at dementia care platform Rippl, and she held senior executive roles at Aetna, naviHealth and Evolent Health. "Drawing on this experience, Sharp will advance clinical outcomes and care model transformation at Strive," company executives remarked in a press release.

Rigg most recently served as chief financial officer and senior vice president of commercial health benefits at Elevance Health, supporting more than 32 million consumers across individual and employer group projects. In his early career, he was a healthcare-focused analyst at Deutsche Bank, Susquehanna International Group and Merrill Lynch.

"Sharp and Rigg’s leadership will help accelerate Strive’s ability to deliver measurable outcomes for patients, providers and payers as Strive continues to expand its value-based kidney care model nationwide," Chris Riopelle, CEO and co-founder, stated in a statement.

In a recent development, >R1, a healthcare revenue management leader, unveiled that Eric Tagliere will join the manufacturer as Chief Information Officer. During his over 30-year career, Tagliere has served as Chief Technology Officer for both Humana and Marriott, leading both companies’ technological integration.

In a recent development, at Humana, Tagliere spearheaded operations to advance their cloud and technology modernization strategy, according to the company’s press release. At Marriott, he was a key part of the technological integration of Starwood Hotels & Resorts and oversaw digital engineering. In his newly introduced role at R1, Tagliere will assist in R1’s transformation “from a labor-first to technology-first paradigm.” This work is in line with R1’s pioneering Healthcare Revenue Operating System that combines AI with human intelligence to improve the revenue cycle.

In his statement, Chief Executive Officer of R1, Joe Flanagan states, “I am pleased to welcome Eric to R1 as we continue to strengthen our technology capabilities and position the Firm for long-term, AI-enabled growth. With more than three decades of experience leading large-scale technology transformations, Eric is a proven leader who brings unique insights and capabilities to advance our technology strategy.”.

> The American Medical Association has named Sandra Adamson Fryhofer, M.D., as its next president-elect, a decision that comes as the current holder of that title, Willie Underwood III, M.D., takes the place of outgoing president Bobby Mukkamala, M.D.

Sources indicate that fryhofer has been a prominent voice in public health. Alongside serving as the AMA's liaison to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (CDC ACIP), she has been a regular medical correspondent and contributor for CNN and Medscape.

"We have a tremendous opportunity to improve public health and ensure every patient has access to high-quality care. I am honored to serve as president-elect as we continue that work together.”.

Recent findings suggest that >Rajneesh Kumar is joining Staritas, an independent health supply chain data provider, as the company's new Chief Technology Officer. Recent findings suggest that >Ben Nielsen will succeed the retiring CEO of Ridgeview Medical Center, Mike Phelps. Sources indicate that >Anant Vinjamoori, M.D., will serve as the new Chief Medical Officer for the Hims brand, an online comprehensive care platform. Industry observers note that >The Melanoma Research Alliance (MRA), a nonprofit funder of melanoma research, declared that beginning on July 1, 2026, Stephanie Kauffmann will serve as the organization's Chief Executive Officer. >Ardent Health President and CEO Marty Bonick "has stepped down to pursue other opportunities," the for-profit health system announced this week. Replacing him immediately is Dave Caspers, who had been serving as chief operating officer.

It has been revealed that bonick helmed the organization through a string of challenges, including the COVID-19 pandemic and its 2024 initial public offering. Board Chairman Mark Sotir noted that work in the announcement and said the former head executive had positioned Ardent "for sustained long-term growth and help[ed] build a strong foundation as the Company continues to navigate industry headwinds with a focus on disciplined execution. Caspers, meanwhile, joined Ardent in March 2025 but has spent decades in operational roles. These include senior healthcare leadership positions at Walmart Health, Banner Health and Target. He's spent the past year in the weeds of Ardent's IMPACT (Improve Margins, Performance, Agility and Care Transformation) Program.

"Today, Ardent Health and our best-in-class team are well-positioned to accelerate our next phase of growth, and I am eager to build on this momentum with a continued focus on delivering high-quality care to the communities we serve.”.

>Drew Altman, M.D., founding president and CEO of the influential heath policy research, polling and news nonprofit KFF, will retire from his roles at the end of this year.

He formed the organization in 1990 out of the Henry J. Kaiser Family Foundation, and has since expanded its scope to include the country's largest newsroom focused on health policy, KFF Health News.

“With two small grandkids in Sacramento and Atlanta and another on the way, after what will be almost 37 years of very hands-on leadership since I founded KFF, and with KFF at the apex of its effectiveness, and the opportunity for a perfect transition, the clock in my head is telling me it’s time,” Altman said in this week's announcement.

Following the recommendation of a search committee, KFF has unanimously appointed two in-house leaders to take on Altman's titles: Larry Levitt, right now executive vice president for health policy, as CEO; and Mollyann Brodie, Ph.D., currently executive vice president and chief operating officer, as president.

According to recent reports, the pair have a combined six decades of experience at KFF already under their belt, and will take on board positions with their newly introduced roles. They will work with Altman to ensure a smooth transition through the end of the year, officially stepping into his shoes in January 2027.

>Visory Health, a prescription savings program, has promoted two executives: Alexandra Robertson to chief growth officer, and Brittney Tierce to chief technology officer.

Recent findings suggest that "Technology should be a bridge, not a barrier," Tierce said in the announcement. "My focus is raising that bar continuously by creating smarter systems, faster delivery and infrastructure that scales access to the communities we serve.".

Sources indicate that abridge is rapidly scaling its AI scribe and clinical decision support technology. It is live in more than 270 of the largest health systems in the U.S., including Duke Health, Johns Hopkins Medicine, Sutter Health and Yale Newly introduced Haven Health. It has been revealed that "I've spent my career building products and platforms that people love to use that are secure and reliable. > Jeff Balser, M.D., Ph.D., is retiring from his roles as CEO of Vanderbilt Health and dean of Vanderbilt University School of Medicine at the end of 2026.

The academic system's board of directors has kicked of a national search for a successor who would hold both titles, according to the March 12 announcement.

Recent findings suggest that A 1990 Vanderbilt graduate himself, Balser spent years as a cardiac anesthesiologist and surgical intensivist at Johns Hopkins before returning to Vanderbilt in 1998. He was named chair of the Department of Anesthesiology in 2001, dean of the medical school in 2008 and head of the Vanderbilt University Medical Center in 2009. He has served as dean and in the health system's top executive role for the past 17 years.

The organization has grown from a four-hospital system to an eight-hospital system under his tenure, during which its annual net revenue also grew from around $2 billion to nearly $9 billion, according to the announcement. Part of that time was an effort he led to legally and financially separate the medical center and its system from the university as a standalone nonprofit. The organization's cash reserves also have also grown from 50 days to more than 110, with total cash on hand plus investments now exceeding $3 billion.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes
CMS proposes sweeping Medicare integrity rule it says will save $90B" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services rolled out a newly introduced proposed rule it said could save $90 billion over ten years through increased oversight and prevention of fraud and improper payments.

It has been revealed that the Comprehensive Regulations to Uncover Suspicious Healthcare (CRUSH) proposed rule, shared late Monday, spans Medicare, Medicaid, the Children’s Health Insurance Program (CHIP) and the Health Insurance Marketplace. It follows a request for information the administration circulated back in February. CMS it intends to conduct similar program integrity rulemaking “on an annual basis going forward.”.

Among the highlights: stiffer provider screening and safeguards for Medicare enrollment, a latest regulatory framework for reporting and returning self-identified Medicaid fee-for-service overpayments similar to those in other programs, and requirements that Medicaid managed care looks report beneficiary deaths or address changes within 30 days to help CMS better spot improper payments.

“When President Trump called upon the federal government to crush fraud, waste, and abuse, CMS got right to work, using every tool at its disposal to achieve historic savings,” CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz, M.D., mentioned in the agency’s announcement of the proposed rule. “CRUSH would build on those results by giving us stronger tools to prevent fraud, remove bad actors, and protect the Americans who rely on these programs. Whether criminals are billing Medicare for nonexistent canes and wheelchairs, fraudulently enrolling healthy seniors in Medicare-funded hospice care, or signing people up for Marketplace prepares without their consent, the CRUSH proposed rule would give CMS stronger authority to stop these schemes and hold those responsible accountable.”.

The additional guardrails are expected to cost the government about $378.5 million over the same 10-year period CMS expects to save nearly $90 billion, according to the proposed rule.

Recent findings suggest that CMS, in its release and a lengthy fact sheet outlining the proposed changes, said it wants to update Medicare provisions to tighten Medicare Advantage (MA) Adjustment Data Validation audits so that it can better spot cases in which diagnoses are not supported by medical documentation, thereby bumping up risk scores and payments. It also wants to increase suspicious activity reporting requirements for MA organizations and Part D plan sponsors, require some MA plan providers and suppliers to also enroll in Original Medicare for credential verification and guard seniors from unsolicited outreach from medical supply companies.

According to recent reports, in Medicaid and CHIP, the agency wants to make it easier for states to join in on suspected schemes while fleshing out their data collection and reporting. CMS also wants to add provider enrollment termination grounds similar to those in Medicare.

In a recent development, within the marketplace, CMS said it wants to begin restricting access for agents and brokers with certain felony convictions or other healthcare program exclusions on their record. The agency is also looking to bolster its authority to suspend and terminate, and to do so more quickly.

According to recent reports, “President Trump directed us to stop fraud, waste, and abuse, and the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services is taking action to protect taxpayer dollars,” HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. remarked in the announcement. “CRUSH would give CMS stronger tools to block fraudulent payments, remove dishonest providers, and protect Americans from schemes that exploit their healthcare coverage.

Public comment on the proposed rule, which includes more potential changes and a breakdown of the expected savings and costs, will be open through Jan. 19, 2027.

The program integrity proposed rule landed the same day CMS released its estimates on improper payments during fiscal year 2026.

In a recent development, improper payments are those that do not meet the agency’s program requirements, and can include overpayments or underpayments alike. They are not necessarily a measure of fraud, though “some improper payments may involve fraud or abuse” alongside administrative errors, CMS noted.

Sources indicate that in total, the agency outlined about $112.9 billion in estimated overpayments, an increase over the roughly $96.1 billion estimated for the prior fiscal year. That broke down into:.

CMS noted that the estimates are tied to claims submitted from July 1, 2024 through June 30, 2025, a period “before many of CMS’ current crushing fraud initiatives were implemented.” Those and other efforts will begin appearing in next year’s improper payment data, it said.

Recent findings suggest that word has just dropped that the mega-hit sci-fi film “Project Hail Mary” has returned to the substantial screen for the holiday season with its nail-biting tale of science, adventure and friendship. Catch a brand new Hail Mary trailer on YouTube while the action heats up here on Earth, including solicitations for the next class of astronauts, the formation of the new US Space Academy, and next steps for the Artemis mission to the Moon.

On November 7, NASA (the National Aeronautics and Space Administration) began taking applications for the next class of astronauts. The deadline is 11:59 PM ET on December 3.

NASA received more than 8,000 applications during the last round of astronaut recruitment, in 2024. Only 10 candidates were selected — but don’t be discouraged. Just look at the payoff as described by NASA:.

The next generation of astronauts will train to operate on the lunar surface, live and work beyond Earth, and take on missions that will push the boundaries of human exploration farther than ever before.

Recent findings suggest that “The next generation of astronaut candidates could help write history while inspiring future scientists, engineers, and explorers,” adds Scott Tingle, chief astronaut and chair of the NASA Astronaut Selection Board. Interested? Apply here.

Sources indicate that if you blinked, you missed the formation of the latest US Space Academy. However, the folks over at the Louisiana Economic Development agency were on the ball. On November 12, LED revealed that Louisiana has thrown its hat into the ring for the privilege of hosting the the forthcoming Space Academy.

“The Space Academy is a proposed NASA-supported federal academy that will educate the next generation of astronauts, engineers, scientists, and leaders for America’s space programs,” LED explains.

If all goes according to initiative, the first Space Academy class will occupy Louisiana State University in New Orleans with a roster of 300 students in the fall of 2028, with room for a total of 4,000 — or more — to follow.

According to recent reports, if you’re wondering why Louisiana thinks it has a good shot at hosting such an endeavor, Louisiana Governor Jeff Landry summarized the case in a press statement. “The United States Space Academy belongs in a state that builds the rockets, supports our nation’s military and is now home to the world’s largest spaceport,” Landry enthused.

Sources indicate that as described in an LED press release, the state’s qualifications include hosting “America’s Rocket Factory,” aka the Michoud Assembly Facility in Fresh Orleans. The facility is owned by NASA and managed by the Marshall Space Flight Center, which among other projects has just released a new album of “baby star sounds.”.

The idea of a dedicated center for space education and training bubbled up from the White House just a few months ago, in August. NASA promptly jumped on it, inviting the governors of all 50 states to compete for the new facility.

Industry observers note that louisiana is determined to beat them all to the punch. With LED in the lead, collaborators on the state’s Space Academy proposal include Louisiana State University, the City of Latest Orleans, the business organization Greater New Orleans, Inc., and the New Orleans subsidiary of the leading utility Entergy among others, with all of the state’s US Senators and Representatives enlisted in support.

“A dedicated state fund, the Louisiana U.S. Space Academy Fund, will cover startup needs and independent operating infrastructure, lowering the federal investment needed to launch and sustain the Academy,” LED adds, noting that two other schools — Southern University at Fresh Orleans and Tulane University — are also lending their support to the LSU campus.

LED and its partners are leaning heavily on the presence of the Michoud Assembly Facility to leverage its claim to host the Space Academy. As LED notes, Michoud has been front and center in crewed space flight for 65 years, and it sits only about nine miles from the LSU campus.

“Michoud built the Saturn V first stages for Apollo, every Space Shuttle external tank, and the core stages for the Space Launch System rockets that power NASA’s Artemis missions,” LED explains.

“The National Center for Advanced Manufacturing at Michoud develops the composite and metallic manufacturing processes behind that hardware,” the agency adds.

Recent findings suggest that LED Secretary Susan B. Bourgeois also chipped in her two cents. “Louisiana is building one of the most consequential aerospace ecosystems in the country, and the U.S. Space Academy would give us the opportunity to build the talent pipeline alongside it,” Bourgeois remarked.

“Cadets would learn alongside leaders in government and commercial and space, including NASA’s Michoud Assembly Center and Stennis Space Center, SpaceX Starbase Louisiana, Michoud tenants including Boeing, Lockheed Martin, Textron Systems, and Vivace,” LED elaborates, also taking note of the presence of the Naval Information Warfare Center among other resources.

“Greater New Orleans anchors the middle of America’s southern space corridor, which runs from Kennedy Space Center at Cape Canaveral to Johnson Space Center in Houston and SpaceX’s Starbase in South Texas, with Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville to the north,” LED adds again for good measure.

As for the Artemis mission, as of October NASA seemed pretty optimistic about the chances for sending people to the Moon sooner rather than later. A newly introduced schedule calls for an Artemis III test flight in Earth orbit next year. The flight will include shakeouts of docking and other systems between NASA’s Orion spacecraft and lunar landers from both from SpaceX and Blue Origin.

“Four astronauts will fly aboard Orion, released on NASA’s SLS (Space Launch System) rocket, for a planned 14-day mission in Earth orbit to reduce risk ahead of the Artemis IV moon landing mission,” NASA explained.

Sources indicate that “The Artemis III mission will unfold in sequence,” NASA explained. “Blue Origin will launch a Blue Moon lander test article into Earth orbit, SLS will launch Orion and its crew, docking with the Blue Moon lander test article, then SpaceX will launch a Version 3 Starship lander test article while Orion will undock from Blue Moon and dock with Starship.”.

Assuming that all goes off without a hitch, 2028 will see US astronauts on walking on the Moon, presumably before anybody else gets there.

Industry observers note that the last time US citizens set foot on the Moon, millions of Terrestrials witnessed the fuzzy, flickering action on live TV. If you were among them, share the experience in the discussion thread What was it like? Did everyone cheer? Or did somebody say something random such as “I need a cigarette,” and is that the moment that burns especially bright in your memory? Asking for a friend….

Google Ads Quality Score is essentially a measurement of the quality and relevance of both your keywords and PPC ads. It is a dynamic metric, assigned on a scale of 1 to 10, with 10 being the best possible score. It is used by Google to determine your cost per click (CPC) and your ad rank in the ad auction process.

Quality Score is calculated based on three primary components: click-through rate (CTR), ad relevance, and landing page experience.

Recent findings suggest that for any industry, including real estate, a good Quality Score is generally around 7 or above. However, in the competitive world of real estate, striving for an even higher Quality Score could give you an advantage. So, for realtors, a great Quality Score might be considered 8 or above.

That said, keep in mind that a high-Quality Score is not an end in itself. It's a sign that your ads are relevant, and your landing pages provide a good user experience, but it's still just one factor in the overall success of your Google Ads campaigns.

A high-Quality Score is beneficial for several reasons:.

There is a growing consensus that Europe must reduce its reliance on Chinese cleantech, especially batteries.

The IAA marks a major shift in EU industrial policy. It introduces Union content incentives to ensure scarce public subsidies and corporate tax incentives are used to support European manufacturing. This demand-side pull is crucial if the energy transition is to deliver high-value industrial jobs and lessen critical geopolitical dependencies. There is a growing consensus that Europe must reduce its reliance on Chinese cleantech, especially batteries. But several proposals at the moment before co-legislators risk severely undermining that overarching goal. Diluting battery criteria in the IAA means giving up on a strategic value chain for Europe, leaving it to China only.

T&E’s assessment shows that only an IAA with a calibrated timeline, robust battery requirements and a strict geographical scope will deliver substantial benefits for Europe. Without secured demand, announced industrial capacity will simply not materialise.

The Franco-German automotive deal from 16 October 2026 is a major blow for Europe’s battery industry as it severely dilutes incentives for batteries. It suggests battery sourcing requirements for eligible vehicles of 10% in 2028-2029, 20% in 2030-2031 and 70% from 2032 on. This is far below what the market already does: over 50% of cells in electric vehicles (EVs) sold in the EU are already Made-in-Europe. By 2030, the deal would only secure 13% (62 GWh) of Europe’s announced cell production: a further 206 GWh would likely find European buyers, though with no guarantee, while 220 GWh would find no demand at all. Even in 2032, the 70% would still not secure a substantial share of potential cell capacity (only 45%).

Another major risk is applying a wide Made-with-EU geographical scope to battery criteria. Compared to a strict EU-only scope, including free trade agreement (FTA) partners puts around 100 GWh of cell demand and 250 GWh of cathode active materials (CAM) demand at risk of leakage in 2030. Limiting the scope to trusted partners only helps to a limited extent. Since Europe can produce enough cells to meet demand under a Made-in-EU IAA, adding partner countries risks leaving EU production without offtakers: even with trusted partners only, a third of potential EU cell supply could be affected. For CAM, around 30% of expected EU supply could be left without a buyer under a trusted-partners scope, rising to 50% under an extended one.

It has been revealed that the midstream, CAM and their precursors (pCAM), is the weakest link in Europe’s battery value chain. Boosting this key segment and diversifying away from China is essential for resilience as it shields European industry from supply disruptions and export controls. Under a strict Made-in-EU scope, reaching IAA CAM requirements is technically and commercially viable by 2030, requiring only limited sourcing from trusted partners (33 GWh cell-equivalent). From 2032, EU production can cover demand from EVs under support schemes. A Made-in-EU IAA would generate 323 GWh of extra EU CAM demand in 2032, around the output of six mid-sized EU CAM plants, bringing total EU-made CAM to 407 GWh (securing 94% of expected EU supply).

pCAM is just as vital for resilience and to establish local offtake for European refiners and recyclers. A 28% EU pCAM requirement in 2032 applied to a carmaker’s entire fleet sales (not only for vehicles eligible for public support) creates enough demand for expected EU supply to materialise and projects to reach Final Investment Decision (FID). Onshoring CAM and pCAM adds only a modest cost of $10.6/kWh for Nickel Manganese Cobalt (NMC) and $6.5/kWh for Lithium Iron Phosphate (LFP) batteries. This is a necessary sovereignty premium that will fall as the EU supply chain matures.

Industry observers note that the car CO₂ standards are as critical to industrial delivery as the IAA. Even under a strict Made-in-EU scope, the European Parliament’s position as approved by the leading committee in November 2026 would sharply cut expected EV sales and reduce EU cell demand by 247 GWh between 2027 and 2032, which equals 3.7 million EU made EVs.

Industry observers note that finally, the proposed fleet booster mechanism fails to drive industrial onshoring and relocation if its compliance trigger is set below 85%. Carmakers’ efforts to lower that threshold aim at getting a stamp of approval on their sourcing strategy in China. A major risk for public subsidies ending up benefiting imported cars with Chinese batteries. Attempts to lower the Booster below a 85% threshold should be rejected, especially if combined with weaker battery criteria.

It’s key to reject the Franco-German deal proposal on batteries.

Battery criteria in this deal are too weak to create additional demand and undermine the IAA’s core purpose.

By Franziska Grüning, Raw Materials OfficerBrussels (EU), T&E.

Jordane Faizant, Analyst, FleetsBrussels (EU).

Jeanne Andre, Analyst, Raw MaterialsBrussels (EU).
