Heidi Overton’s FDA nomination pulled by White House" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The White House pulled the nomination for Heidi Overton, M.D., Ph.D., to lead the FDA just hours before the Senate was scheduled to vote on her confirmation.

The move hardly comes as a surprise after Overton’s confirmation hearing before the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions (HELP) Committee drew contention.

It has been revealed that the news was first reported by Axios on Tuesday evening. The White House confirmed the news to Fierce the following morning.

In September, the HELP committee questioned Overton in a hearing marked by tightrope-walking on concerns like vaccines, abortions, flavored vapes and whether or not President Donald Trump is capable of being wrong.

Overton conceded multiple times during the hearing that vaccines approved by the FDA, as well as the “abortion pill” mifepristone, are safe and effective. But she stopped short of admitting that Trump has been wrong when dispensing medical information out of line with what scientific evidence demonstrates.

Overton’s nomination faced mounting pushback and uncertainty from senators ahead of a planned HELP Committee vote on Nov. 18. Fierce reached out to Sen. Ed Markey, the veteran Democratic lawmaker from Massachusetts, ahead of the vote, and he told Fierce that he would “vote against her nomination, and I urge my colleagues to do the same.”.

“The FDA needs a leader who will stand up for science and for our kids’ safety, not one who stood by while both were undermined,” he added.

Recent findings suggest that republican Sen. Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, who chairs the Senate health committee, and other Republicans had also raised questions about Overton's nomination.

As support for Overton looked thin, Republicans were discussing Sen. Roger Marshall, a Kansas Republican, as a potential replacement, Semafor reported today. Health Secretary Kennedy reportedly met with Marshall in recent days to discuss filling the role, according to Politico, but the White House told the publication that it is not considering him.

Sources indicate that robert Steinbrook, M.D., health research group director for Public Citizen, commented today urging the HELP committee to reject Overton’s nomination: “The FDA needs a strong commissioner who stands for science and the integrity of the agency,” Steinbrook noted. “Overton is the wrong choice for FDA Commissioner and has done nothing to dispel the well-founded reasons to oppose her candidacy.”.

Analysts from Citi shared that the White House’s decision to pull the nomination has a negative impact on biopharma, “extending uncertainty around permanent agency leadership.”.

“We view the withdrawal as a modest sentiment negative, but not a material near-term change to the regulatory environment facing most drug and biologics sponsors,” the analysts mentioned in the note.

The withdrawal of Overton's nomination leaves a gap at an FDA that has already faced significant upheaval. The White House only shifted its focus to Overton in August, after the agency had spent three months without a permanent leader.

Since former FDA commissioner Marty Makary, M.D., departed the agency in May, Kyle Diamantas, who hails from the agency’s food regulation division, has been at the helm in an interim capacity.

#6762. Alzheimer’s may have early warning signs outside the brain

Alzheimer’s may have early warning signs outside the brain

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1466 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Alzheimer's disease is best known for its effects on memory and thinking, but new research suggests that some symptoms may develop in a surprising place: outside the brain.
  • Scientists at the University of Central Florida (UCF) have discovered that genetic mutations associated with Alzheimer's can interfere with the nerves that control muscle movement, even without involvement from the brain or spinal cord.
  • The discovery raises the possibility that movement difficulties could provide earlier warning signs of the disease and that treatments focused exclusively on the brain may overlook vital problems elsewhere in the body.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Alzheimer's disease is best known for its effects on memory and thinking, but new research suggests that some symptoms may develop in a surprising place: outside the brain.

Scientists at the University of Central Florida (UCF) have discovered that genetic mutations associated with Alzheimer's can interfere with the nerves that control muscle movement, even without involvement from the brain or spinal cord. The findings could help explain why some people with Alzheimer's experience changes in walking, balance, or coordination long before noticeable memory problems emerge.

The discovery raises the possibility that movement difficulties could provide earlier warning signs of the disease and that treatments focused exclusively on the brain may overlook vital problems elsewhere in the body.

Recent findings suggest that the research was led by James Hickman, a professor at UCF's Nanoscience Technology Center, and Research Professor Xiufang "Nadine" Guo, working alongside scientists at the healthcare technology organization Hesperos. Funded by the National Institutes of Health's National Institute on Aging, the study used laboratory systems built from human cells to investigate how inherited Alzheimer's mutations affect movement. The findings were published in Alzheimer's & Dementia: The Journal of the Alzheimer's Association.

Recent findings suggest that "Motor deficits may be an earlier indication [of Alzheimer's]," Guo notes. "If we can detect those changes and intervene earlier, that could help delay the onset of central nervous system symptoms.".

Why Alzheimer's Symptoms May Appear Before Memory Loss.

Sources indicate that alzheimer's is generally associated with progressive memory loss, confusion, and declining cognitive abilities. However, doctors have also observed that some patients develop physical symptoms, including changes in balance, coordination, and gait (manner of walking), years before clear cognitive difficulties become apparent.

These observations have raised an crucial question: Are such movement problems simply a consequence of damage occurring in the brain, or could Alzheimer's also interfere directly with nerves elsewhere in the body?

To investigate, the UCF team focused on familial Alzheimer's, a rare inherited form of the disease that typically develops earlier in life (from 40 to 65 years of age) than the more common form.

Their experiments revealed that motor neurons carrying mutations linked to familial Alzheimer's could disrupt the connections responsible for controlling muscles, even when the brain and spinal cord were completely absent from the experimental system.

Motor neurons are specialized nerve cells that transmit signals to muscles, telling them when to contract and produce movement. The new findings suggest that Alzheimer's mutations can interfere with this process directly, rather than affecting movement only through damage to the brain.

In a recent development, "This is the first time it's been demonstrated that deficits in the peripheral nervous system can arise directly from these mutations," Hickman states. "It means drugs that target the brain may not fix problems in the rest of the body.".

The peripheral nervous system includes the nerves located outside the brain and spinal cord. These nerves carry signals between the central nervous system and the rest of the body, helping control movement, sensation, and other essential functions.

Guo also points out that preserving the ability to move could have benefits beyond physical health. Regular physical activity is associated with better cognitive well-being, so protecting motor function may also help support brain health.

How a Miniature Human Cell System Revealed the Discovery.

To examine the relationship between Alzheimer's mutations and muscle movement, the scientists used an innovative laboratory platform known as "human-on-a-chip" technology.

Developed and manufactured through Hesperos, a tech giant co-founded by Hickman, these miniature systems bring different types of human cells together under controlled conditions. They allow researchers to recreate specific biological functions and observe how diseases interfere with them.

Unlike conventional laboratory experiments that examine isolated cells, these systems can reproduce vital interactions between different tissues. They also provide an alternative to animal models, which do not always accurately reflect how human diseases behave.

For this study, the team created a miniature model of the neuromuscular junction, the connection where a motor neuron communicates with a muscle cell.

Recent findings suggest that the model was deliberately designed without a brain or spinal cord. This was a crucial part of the experiment because it allowed the researchers to investigate whether Alzheimer's-related changes could cause movement problems independently of the central nervous system.

Industry observers note that the scientists combined healthy muscle cells with motor neurons derived from stem cells that carried genetic mutations associated with familial Alzheimer's disease. Stem cells are cells that can develop into specialized types of cells, making them valuable tools for studying human diseases in the laboratory.

The researchers then examined how effectively the altered nerve cells communicated with otherwise healthy muscle tissue.

The results showed that the Alzheimer's-associated mutations could interfere with normal nerve-to-muscle function. This suggests that at least some movement difficulties linked to the disease may arise directly in the peripheral nervous system rather than being caused entirely by degeneration in the brain.

Why Damaged Nerve Connections Can Affect Walking and Balance.

Every voluntary movement depends on successful communication between the nervous system and the muscles.

At the neuromuscular junction, an electrical signal traveling along a motor neuron triggers chemical communication that causes a muscle to contract. This process makes everyday activities possible, from walking and maintaining posture to lifting objects and performing precise movements.

In a recent development, when the connection becomes impaired, muscles may respond less effectively to nerve signals. Depending on the severity and location of the problem, this can contribute to weakness, reduced coordination, and difficulty sustaining physical activity.

To evaluate these effects, the research team measured how consistently nerve signals produced muscle contractions and how long the muscles could continue contracting before becoming fatigued.

It has been revealed that these measurements provided a direct assessment of how well the nerve and muscle cells worked together. They also resemble aspects of the functional testing physicians use when examining patients with movement disorders.

According to recent reports, "You can't move unless the motor circuit works," Hickman notes. "When a doctor taps your knee to check your reflex, they're testing that exact connection.".

By demonstrating impaired nerve-to-muscle communication in a system containing no brain or spinal cord, the study provides evidence that mutations linked to familial Alzheimer's can produce effects beyond the central nervous system.

Recent findings suggest that however, the experiments do not establish that these changes necessarily occur before memory loss in patients. Further research will be needed to determine how closely the laboratory findings reflect the progression of Alzheimer's in people, particularly those with the more common forms of the disease.

Could This Discovery Lead to Earlier Alzheimer's Detection?

The findings suggest a potentially important new direction for Alzheimer's research: looking beyond memory and other cognitive symptoms when investigating the disease.

If future studies confirm that changes in motor function are detectable early in certain patients, tests of walking, coordination, or nerve-to-muscle activity might eventually help identify disease-related changes before more obvious neurological symptoms develop.

Recent findings suggest that the results also raise questions about treatment. Many Alzheimer's therapies are designed to address processes occurring in the brain, but medications that target the central nervous system may not necessarily correct abnormalities affecting peripheral nerves and muscles.

Understanding these separate effects could help researchers investigate treatments that protect physical function alongside cognitive health.

Human-on-a-Chip Technology Could Transform Disease Research.

Beyond the implications for Alzheimer's, the researchers see considerable potential in using human-on-a-chip systems to investigate other diseases and evaluate possible treatments.

Because these platforms contain human cells and reproduce measurable biological activities, they can help scientists observe disease-related changes in conditions that more closely resemble human physiology than some conventional experimental models.

This approach may be particularly useful in drug development, where researchers need to understand not only how a potential treatment affects individual cells but also how it influences interactions between different tissues.

Such systems can also uncover biological effects that may be difficult to detect in animal experiments, potentially helping researchers identify promising therapies and recognize limitations earlier in development.

For Hickman, the progress represents the culmination of three decades of work devoted to understanding disease through more realistic laboratory models.

"These systems let us study disease in a way that's closer to what actually happens in the human body, and that's what we need to develop better treatments," he states.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, if you're just reading this, you were likely not one of the 43 enlisted soldiers taking advantage of a four-day leave to play "Grand Theft Auto 6," and instead worked a full day at your job and/or took care of other real-life responsibilities. Being late to the party, though, means there's more insight on the internet for your playthrough, telling you to make sure you fill your gas tank, or remember that Flock-like cameras will track you during your crime sprees. In this case, we found a quicker and easier way to take on one of the first car theft missions in the game.

The mission, called "Unwanted Attention," is to steal a beloved red Phoenix from a police impound lot to acquire some misplaced "cargo," i.e. the "like 20 pounds or something" of weed that Cal tells you is hidden somewhere in the car. According to Polygon, this can be done one of two ways. The first — which is not recommended — is to make your presence very known with weapons and a show. The other, much subtler method is acquisition by stealth.

Now, the version Polygon points you toward is doable, but looks to be pretty involved. Its version has you using special machines to get onto the roof and sneaking into an office where you might have to take down a mechanic. However, a favorite YouTuber of mine found a way that's even more chill, with far fewer steps.

Sources indicate that the fun begins when you pull up to the impound lot in Hamlet. First, you'll want to ensure that Jason doesn't have any weapons on his person. Meanwhile, in gameplay, Cal sends a text: "Help her rise from the flames (fire emoji x3)." Polygon's guide tells you your best bet from here is to not hop the impound lot fence, but if no one is around, you can go ahead and scramble over it, like Jacksepticeye did. From here, casually walk through the little lot to the far back right corner, where you'll see some shipment boxes stacked together in a convenient way that leads up to a storage container on the other side of the fence. Climb up and enjoy a view for a beat.

It's not easy to spot upon first glance, but you'll essentially want to look for the white tow truck under the awning tucked toward the farthest wall from where you are standing. The elusive Phoenix is attached behind it. Carefully climb down from the container and walk casually toward the right of the tow truck. You'll want to be careful to avoid being seen or detected by the cop on the left side of the lot.

According to recent reports, just to be safe, you can use your Waink car scanner on your phone to verify the car attached to the truck is indeed the Phoenix. It'll tell you it's a 1977 Imponte Phoenix (or, in real life, a Pontiac Firebird Trans Am, recognizable thanks to the large gold "Screaming Chicken" on the hood). You can easily unhook the Phoenix from the truck.

According to recent reports, now all you have to do is get in the car and hot-wire it — the game will tell you how to do so. Take the car toward the impound lot gate (where you came in) to open it, which will take a painstaking minute, especially thanks to all of the attention you have now drawn trying to drive the car out of the lot. Once it's open, get going! Keep an eye out, however, with your newly acquired flock of enthusiastic followers: the police.

Industry observers note that GTA gamers will know you just have to keep on driving to lose these guys. Once you do that, the game will find ways to let you know to take the car to the Hamlet Pay 'N' Spray shop, where you can fix your likely very dented car as you get acclimated to the game. You'll also want to give it a little makeover  so as to avoid drawing any additional attention. Then it's time to deliver the finished product to Brian's garage where you'll collect a $150 cash reward, likely to fund your own makeover, as you'll also need a way to be less identifiable to outsmart the cops. With that all done, your mission is finally complete.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Celebrity chef Dook Chase is intentionally never far from a kitchen, be it inside one of his renowned restaurants or his dream family home in Upcoming Orleans.

Chase, 44, is the fourth-generation owner of Dooky Chase’s Restaurant, the legendary culinary destination and cultural institution that’s been operating in the Significant Easy since 1941. The NOLA native also runs his modern Creole eatery, Chapter IV, commuting between both businesses from a Southern-style, two-story residence that he shares with his wife, Gretchen, their daughter, Sidney, and son, Vito.

In a recent development, “It's a seven-minute commute to both restaurants,” Chase tells Realtor.com® in the latest Celebrity Sanctuary. “I can visit each one in its peak time. I can get a text from any server saying, ‘Hey, a table came in that really wanted to see you,’ and I [say], ‘Tell them I'll be there in seven minutes.’ I can hop in the car and get to each.”.

Personally connecting with the local community over a meal is a practice that is baked into Chase’s family backstory and a tradition he proudly upholds today.

Industry observers note that “When you think about Dooky Chase Restaurant and my grandmother, chef Leah Chase, in the time that she helmed that kitchen ... the history of our restaurant is really through the Civil Rights Movement, opening doors to everyone in the community: Blacks and whites, together, at a time when laws didn't allow it. But we always allowed it at our restaurant,” the Le Cordon Bleu-educated executive chef explains. “My grandparents, great-grandparents, [and] certainly my parents understood the importance of learning from each and every person ... and we were able to do that through food.

Industry observers note that “One thing that I love about my family's history and what we've been able to do every Thanksgiving is, we open our restaurant on Thanksgiving Day,” he continues. “So we gather with our community first, and then we close, clean up, set the tables all over again, and then [our] families come in. It’s a way to serve others and then enjoy your day right after.”.

In a recent development, chase’s Thanksgiving menu is typically an “endless” buffet of classic Southern dishes, including his favorite, gumbo, followed by multiple dessert options. However, this year, the “Family Recipe Showdown” star is bringing some fresh inspiration to the table thanks to his time working with fellow chef Christina Tosi and actress Drew Barrymore on the latest “Pillsbury Bake-off Classic” competition show, due to air on Nov. 23 on CBS and Paramount+.

“We have different experiences and different backgrounds, but ... we learn from one another,” Chase indicates. “That's what I enjoyed about this bake-off. This really brings people together and unites them [to] think about the memories of their childhoods, their families, their celebrations, and you felt that in that room.”.

Recent findings suggest that in this edition of Celebrity Sanctuary, Chase welcomes a look at his hospitable kitchen where he often hosts gatherings with family and friends on ordinary and special occasions alike. Plus, he explains how the heart of the 1952-built, 4,400-square-foot, five-bedroom, five-bathroom home helps him focus on the moment he’s in as much as the meal he’s making.

In a recent development, our previous home is a block away from here. I would exercise in the morning, run up and down [this] oak tree–lined street, and I would tell my wife, “If something ever comes up for sale, I'm buying.”.

In a recent development, as I was running one morning, [the previous owner’s] children were putting up a sign, and I asked, “Can you wait a day? Don't put up the sign. Let's talk. And then if it doesn't work, put up a sign.”.

They waited that day. It happened to work out. I think why it worked out was because their father understood the family atmosphere of what he wanted that next owner to be. When we shared the story of who I was and all about my family, it was like, “This is what I want to happen in this house.”.

It's a beautiful house. I really enjoy it ... and am excited to raise my family and the next generation of us here.

In a recent development, the architectural style of this home is Southern Latest Orleans. We have the significant oak tree. We have the brick porch. We have the wood doors. We have shutters.

Sources indicate that I bought this home in 2009, and we moved in 2010. When we got it, it was completely gutted from the devastation of Hurricane Katrina. We renovated it and brought it to where it is today. We added on to the porch to add a newly introduced front door section where you can be greeted by artwork or by us, and then eventually get to the stairs.

In a recent development, one of the great things we were able to do in this house is save some of the original hardwood. The rooms upstairs that didn't have hardwood, that had carpet, we brought [the hardwood] to those rooms, refurbished them, and then downstairs, laid all newly introduced hardwood down. Most of the windows we were able to keep.

In a recent development, downstairs, we wanted to open it up. Back in the day, they had walls where you would walk through a door into the kitchen, so it was closed off to the other rooms. For me as a chef, when I'm cooking, I want to see everybody. It's where people gather, so that kitchen really dictates every movement that's going on downstairs. Whether you're in the living room, the dining room, the den—you can see and smell what's going on in that kitchen.

Sources indicate that sanctuary, for me, it means home. It means peace. It means comfort. It's almost like you're getting a big hug that wraps you and indicates, “I got you.”.

My comfort zone is the kitchen. It's where I find peace. That's where I can block out all the noise and really home in on what's happening right now.

The home kitchen allows you to slow down. It's different timing. There's not 200 people in the dining room waiting for their meals; there might be just three hungry people. It allows you to slow down and to really think and to really enjoy the meal that you're cooking or the meal that you're eating.

Also, we use my home as a test kitchen. We’ve done many cookbooks. Most of those recipes I've tested in my home versus tested in a restaurant, because it allows you to slow down. It allows you to measure. It allows you to take your time and say, “If I was a home cook reading this cookbook, what do I need to have?” It gives me that hybrid space of really focusing and slowing down and getting it right versus having extra things come through in and out of that kitchen. In your home, you really have that peace to enjoy the process.

It has been revealed that we have a big six-burner stove, a griddle, two ovens, all that good stuff. We have a gray backsplash and a stainless-steel hood. A double-door refrigerator.

The countertops are like a granite marble. I have equipment on top of the countertop: We have a mixer. I love nugget ice, so there's a nugget ice machine.

The cabinets are traditional, white cabinets. They have either copper or brass [hardware]. The wall is painted a gray tone. Going into the den has a navy blue. The colors I like ... enhanced by all of my wife's tastes.

Sources indicate that there's a center where I can move a butcher block if we want to roll out any pastry. It's open. It's not an island, but like an island. On the other side, it's a higher top where there’s almost bar seating.

In a recent development, my kitchen overlooks the dining room. There is a little chandelier there. Our table has windows bringing in a natural light that overlooks an oak tree.

Recent findings suggest that to the left of that is a seating area that has beautiful artwork. Art is huge in my family, so we have artwork everywhere. It has four chairs and a sofa, where we have a coffee table, seating, some statues, some other creative art. Then to the right of that, it's the den and another little nook where we keep a bar.

In a recent development, we have enough room for people to move around. Everything has natural light, and it just flows into different rooms, but the kitchen is the center. It's the focal point of the downstairs of my house. When you have a party, the kitchen is always going to be the focal point of it. No matter what's going on in any other room, people gather in the kitchen.

Sources indicate that we have a lot of fun for holidays, a lot of different traditions that we do here. On Christmas Eve, the family gets together and we hang till about 2 in the morning. Crazy, I know, but it's pretty cool.

My family is huge and faith [is] huge, so we certainly have a cross in there that symbolizes it’s a blessing.

I always call the people in my family that are no longer with us our guardian angels, so [I have] symbols all throughout the kitchen that's highlighting both of my grandmothers in different elements. There's a red pot that we may keep on the stove like we keep in the restaurant that my grandmother loved. We never cook with them at the restaurant. We never really cook with them at home. It was always just that showpiece, and she loved it.

Different small things that may have been from different people, whether it was my side or my wife's side, those things give you back memories of those people, so we have that all throughout the house for cherished memories and reminders that they're always with us. They never really leave us. They keep guiding us, and that's what I love about it.

According to recent reports, I'm happy with [the kitchen] as is. I love this house. I think the only changes would be if my two kids, as they get older, they learn how to clean a little better!

According to recent reports, but that's the beautiful thing about our home and many homes. That dining room table services as so many purposes. You're eating there. You're doing homework there. You’re having discussion there. You’re having people over there. So it does tend to get overwhelmed in terms of how it looks, but that's how vital it is. That's how important food is. It's everything. It's learning. It's education. It's who we are. It's culture. It's family time. So I don't mind it.

Breaking: GTA 6 Ultimate Edition Has A Car Upgrade You Can Unlock Right From The Start

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (749 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, like other installments in the long-running and beloved series, "Grand Theft Auto 6" is as much about the autos as it is about the grand theft.
  • According to recent reports, if you want one of the coolest rides in all of gaming, though, you don't have to work very hard.
  • While Ultimate Edition owners are spoiled with perhaps the best-looking car in the game, they still have to work for it just a bit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, like other installments in the long-running and beloved series, "Grand Theft Auto 6" is as much about the autos as it is about the grand theft. Sure, the game has a campaign, and the open-world setting makes it tons of fun to run around and commit crimes. But for some people, the biggest draw has always been Rockstar's sweet, sweet, non-licensed but clearly real-world-inspired cars (and planes, bikes, and boats, of course). Throughout the game, you'll find and unlock car customization options of all types, from decals to lighting and beyond.

According to recent reports, if you want one of the coolest rides in all of gaming, though, you don't have to work very hard. You just have to shell out the extra $20 to get GTA 6 Ultimate Edition. Doing so gets you early-game access to the coveted and beautiful Ganado Retro Build. This is an exclusive customization of player character Jason's personal '70 Ganado, a Ford Ranchero-like pickup truck that's become an instant classic. Of all the cars of GTA 6, the Ganado Retro Build is especially noteworthy because of what it replaces. It's a major glow up from the well-loved, drab-colored Ganado Jason starts the game with.

While Ultimate Edition owners are spoiled with perhaps the best-looking car in the game, they still have to work for it just a bit. No matter which version of the game you buy, you start out with Jason's base Vapid Ganado, which isn't in the best condition. To upgrade to the iconic Retro Build, you'll have to drive the Ganado to a location called Coastal Auto Care, found in Key Lento. Just don't forget to fill up on the way, because cars in "Grand Theft Auto 6" don't have infinite fuel. The player is introduced to Coastal Auto Care early on via a mission, and you can find it on your map by filtering for "Mod Shops.".

You can upgrade your Ganado during the "Just a Scratch" mission, or you can visit Coastal Auto Care any time after completing the mission to apply the upgrade. Once you've driven into the garage's entrance, you get the car customization screen. This screen offers you a choice of different customization options, like cosmetics, bodywork, performance, and interior. Instead of choosing any of those, select the "Pro Builds" tab, which offers you the choice between full kits and wheel kits. For Ultimate Edition players, the Ganado Retro Build kit is found under "Full Kits," and it's free to apply. Unfortunately, this classic design and slick color palette is specific to Jason's Ganado, so you can't bring in other cars and apply the Retro Build kit to them.

In a recent development, once you're cruising around in the sickest car in the game, you'll want to practice defensive driving. GTA 6 has an advanced physics engine for more realistic car crashes, and nobody wants to see such a beautiful car smashed to bits in a fender-bender.

According to recent reports, if you're the type of person who likes to try out every car possible, you'll have your work cut out for you in "GTA 6." There are over 300 different rides you can find throughout the course of the game. Some, like the Declasse Akane (inspired by the Chevy Sonic) are pretty unexciting, albeit still fun to commit major crimes in. Others are breath-takers that can help under-thrilled enthusiasts live their exotic and classic driving dreams.

Recent findings suggest that take the '95 Grotti Cheetah, inspired by the Ferrari Testarossa. This is another Ultimate Edition-only vehicle, but boy is it sick. If you figure you'll probably never drive a real Testarossa without renting one in Vegas, driving the Cheetah around is a fun second-best. Another eye-grabbing option is the obnoxious green Canis Kamacho, inspired by the Jeep Crew Chief 715 concept. It's a solid in-game off-roader that's available in the base game.

In a recent development, for players with aspirations that extend beyond the asphalt, the Shitzu Squalo is a special boat available to owners of the Ultimate Edition of the game. It's based on the Christ-Craft Stinger 390x and can be found at the docks of Washington Beach. It has a striking pink and blue gradient color scheme, and despite its name, it's not squalid at all. You'll also get access to biplanes, jets, helicopters, and even airboats as you play the game, allowing you to explore the world in whatever style fits your fancy.

#6755. Obesity linked to up to 27% lower risk of death in dementia

Obesity linked to up to 27% lower risk of death in dementia

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1303 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that A surprising latest study has found that people who are overweight or obese when diagnosed with dementia tend to live longer than those who have a normal body weight.
  • Industry observers note that researchers from Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health and NYU School of Global Public Health found that body weight at the time of diagnosis may provide key clues about how long someone with dementia is likely to live.
  • In a recent development, the results are particularly intriguing because obesity is well established as a risk factor for several serious health problems, including heart disease and diabetes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that A surprising latest study has found that people who are overweight or obese when diagnosed with dementia tend to live longer than those who have a normal body weight. The findings challenge expectations about the relationship between weight and health, suggesting that carrying extra weight may be associated with an unexpected survival advantage after dementia develops.

Industry observers note that researchers from Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health and NYU School of Global Public Health found that body weight at the time of diagnosis may provide key clues about how long someone with dementia is likely to live. Their findings, published in the Journal of Alzheimer's Disease, also highlight the importance of proper nutrition for people living with the condition.

In a recent development, the results are particularly intriguing because obesity is well established as a risk factor for several serious health problems, including heart disease and diabetes. Being overweight or obese during middle age is also associated with a greater likelihood of developing dementia later in life. However, previous research has suggested that the relationship may reverse once dementia has developed, with higher body weight linked to better survival.

Industry observers note that "Because this finding is somewhat counterintuitive, an crucial question is whether it could simply be an artifact of bias. Our analyses suggest that the major sources of bias we examined do not explain the survival advantage associated with higher weight," remarked corresponding author Yuan Zhang, PhD, assistant professor of Sociomedical Sciences at Columbia Mailman and in the Butler Columbia Aging Center.

Obesity Linked to Up to 27% Lower Risk of Death.

The researchers found substantial differences in survival based on body weight at the time of dementia diagnosis. Compared with individuals in the normal weight range, those who were overweight or obese had a significantly lower risk of death, even after the researchers accounted for smoking, existing medical conditions, and demographic characteristics.

According to recent reports, people classified as overweight (body mass index of 25 to 29.9) had a 16 percent lower risk of death. Those with class 1 obesity (BMI of 30 to 34.9) had an even larger reduction of 27 percent, while individuals with class 2 and 3 obesity (BMI equal to or greater than 35) had a 22 percent lower risk.

Despite these striking differences, the researchers caution that the findings should not be interpreted as a recommendation for people with dementia to gain weight.

According to recent reports, "This doesn't mean that patients with dementia should attempt to become overweight or obese, as our study was not designed to test that question. But our findings do suggest that weight status may serve as a useful prognostic signal for survival at the time of dementia diagnosis. They also support the notion that nutrition is a key factor in the health and survival of people with dementia," said Virginia Chang, associate professor of Social and Behavioral Sciences at NYU School of Global Public Health and the study's first author.

Tracking Weight and Dementia Over 24 Years.

To investigate the connection, Zhang, Chang, and their colleagues examined information from the Health and Retirement Study, a nationally representative research project that follows Americans ages 51 and older.

The team analyzed records collected between 1998 and 2022, focusing on 4,523 participants who did not have dementia when they entered the study but subsequently developed the condition.

Sources indicate that because the data covered such a long period, the researchers could examine how participants' weight changed in the years leading up to their diagnosis. They could also determine their weight when dementia was identified and track their survival afterward.

This extended timeline was especially crucial because scientists have questioned whether the apparent benefit of higher body weight is genuine or simply reflects misleading patterns in the data. One possibility is that having additional fat or muscle gives patients resources that help them withstand the physical effects of dementia. Another is that the association arises from factors that earlier studies did not adequately consider.

Could Weight Loss Explain the Dementia Paradox?

One major concern involves weight loss that occurs before dementia becomes clinically apparent.

Earlier research by Zhang and Chang found that people can begin losing weight as much as 10 years before a dementia diagnosis, with the decline becoming more pronounced as the disease approaches.

Recent findings suggest that this creates a potential problem for studies that measure weight only at the time dementia is diagnosed. Some individuals classified as having a normal weight may previously have been heavier and lost weight because of the developing disease. If those individuals are already experiencing more advanced illness, they may face a greater risk of death, making higher body weight appear beneficial by comparison.

It has been revealed that the researchers also considered other possible distortions. Restricting an analysis to people who develop dementia can create misleading relationships between obesity and mortality, even when the underlying connection is more complicated.

Another concern is known as "survivor" bias. Since people with obesity face an increased risk of dying from certain illnesses before reaching the age when dementia typically develops, those who survive long enough to receive a dementia diagnosis may represent an unusually healthy group.

To determine whether these factors explained the findings, the team performed additional analyses designed to evaluate several potential sources of bias. The results indicated that the biases they examined were unlikely to be major drivers of the observed connection between higher weight and lower mortality.

Why Extra Weight Might Help People With Dementia.

Although the precise explanation remains unknown, the researchers identified several biological reasons why additional body weight could be advantageous for someone already living with dementia.

One possibility involves the body's energy reserves. People with more stored fat or greater muscle mass may be better equipped to withstand periods of poor nutrition and the physical deterioration that can accompany the disease.

Dementia can interfere with eating in several ways. Changes in brain function may reduce appetite or motivation to eat, while some patients experience increased energy needs or gradually lose the ability to feed themselves. Over time, these problems can contribute to significant weight loss, muscle wasting, and declining health.

According to recent reports, "Nutrition can be a significant problem for people with dementia," stated Chang. "They may experience wasting and an inability to eat, which can be due to changes in the brain's central drive, leading to loss of appetite and initiative, increased energy expenditure, and difficulties feeding themselves.".

Having additional energy stores or muscle tissue could potentially help patients cope with these challenges, although the study did not establish that these factors directly explain the survival differences.

The researchers emphasize that important questions remain unanswered. Even after examining multiple potential biases and identifying plausible biological explanations, they cannot say for certain why overweight and obese participants experienced lower mortality.

Nevertheless, Zhang and Chang believe that weight at the time of a dementia diagnosis could provide valuable information about a patient's likely survival. The results also reinforce the importance of recognizing and addressing nutritional problems in people with dementia.

Additional study authors include Eleanor Hayes-Larson of the University of Southern California and Hui Zheng of the University of Toronto.

The research received funding from the National Institutes of Health (grant numbers R00AG070274, R00AG075317).

  • Recent findings suggest that I’m just going to stick my neck out and say that the eponymous Aptera solar-powered autocycle from the US startup Aptera will attract enough AI-enriched drivers to make a go of it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that whelp, the AI boom has had one positive knock-on effect. It is creating upcoming multi-millionaires by the bushel, any one of whom can afford to splurge on a pricey new electric vehicle. That aside, EV stakeholders in the US are springing back to life after a year-long slumber. Even General Motors is in play, stirring up long lost memories of its 1990’s-era EV1 debacle instead of hiding its head in shame. What’s up with that?

Recent findings suggest that I’m just going to stick my neck out and say that the eponymous Aptera solar-powered autocycle from the US startup Aptera will attract enough AI-enriched drivers to make a go of it. The on-again, off-again, on-again automaker has been on this year, working towards volume production of a plug-in, three-wheeled two-seater EV that can travel up to 40 miles on its own solar-plus-storage system (see more Aptera news here).

It has been revealed that autocycles were once common here in the US and overseas markets, distinguished from motorcycles by their front-facing seats and steering wheels, rather than straddled seats and handlebars. They fell out of favor in the US by the middle of the 20th century, but 21st century hot-rodders have revived the form with a focus on eyebrow-raising, open-air, gas-guzzling showpieces. In particular, interest has spread in states that do not require autocycle drivers to invest in an additional motorcycle license.

Industry observers note that the Aptera is showy in its own right, resembling a rocket ship with unique aerodynamic styling. Perhaps it may even show up in the next James Bond adventure with James Pattinson at the wheel. In the meantime, the organization has just made good on its pledge to reward early investors in the world’s first solar-powered car with the first production models to role off the assembly line. Aptera #1 goes to the founder and CEO of GDP Venture, Martin Hartono, aka “Accelerator #1.”.

According to recent reports, drivers can reserve an Aptera of their own for just $100, and they can expect to pay about $40,000 for the ride. Considering that the solar fuel is free, anyone in the mood for a head-turning ride will get quite a bargain for their $40,000 compared to other competitors in the zero emission two-seater field, such as the recently refreshed Tesla Roadster.

It has been revealed that speaking of refresh, General Motors has been weirdly lavishing attention on the EV1 sedan all this year, even though the automaker has been roundly criticized for the killing the short-lived car in its cradle. The automaker began producing EV1 electric sedans starting in 1996, following the unveiling of its Impact electric concept car in 1990. Unlike the Impact, EV1 was designed for use on the road. However, it was also designed mainly for the California market, and primarily for lease, not for sale. Production halted in 2003 at just about 1,000 vehicles, all to be recalled by GM and sent to the crusher as chronicled in Chris Paine’s 2006 documentary, “Who Killed The Electric Car?”.

In a recent development, or, maybe not so weird after all. GM’s electrification journey long predates the launch of Tesla Motors in 2003. The legacy automaker is now determined to stake out its claim on automotive history, with 2026 marking the 30th anniversary of the start of EV1 production.

GM has been celebrating the anniversary all this year with multiple long form articles about the Impact and EV1 on its website, eager to remind everybody that its industry-leading vehicle electrification efforts of the 1990’s continue to manifest decades later, in the form of heat pumps for climate control, by-wire technology, and regenerative braking among other elements.

GM’s latest love letter to the EV1 popped up on November 17, when the automaker officially celebrated the completed restoration of the EV1 “V212” alongside its a private owner, Billy Caruso. The rare survivor of GM’s the junkyard crusher was evidently hiding out in an impound lot in Georgia all these years, until Caruso acquired it at auction and enlisted Jared Pink of the popular show The Questionable Garage to fix it up. Considering TQG’s large following on YouTube, GM wisely lent its engineers to the effort, along with several donated parts from its own EV1.

Sources indicate that US President Donald Trump and the Republican majority in Congress have made a heroic effort to dial down the vehicle electrification movement, but facts on the ground keep getting in their way. For starters, today’s advanced batteries apply across multiple energy resources, fossil and non-fossil alike. So, it’s no surprise to see the US Department of Energy continuing to throw taxpayer dollars at newly introduced energy storage projects (here’s one example), even though some of that activity will eventually ripple into the vehicle electrification field.

It has been revealed that the US Department of Defense is also getting into the act. DoD’s electrification journey has been a tedious one, but in recent years it has begun creeping stealthily towards a vision of ground mobility enabled by electricity, providing the key tactical advantages of silent running and a low heat signature.

The latest news on that score involves a $1.4 billion loan commitment from DoD’s Office of Strategic Capital (OSC), enabling the silicon-based battery materials startup Sila to vault its signature product into commercial production. DoD’s primary interest in the tech giant consists of applications in the electric drone and autonomous mobility fields, but Sila has long been eyeballing the EV market as well.

In a recent development, sila secured the loan commitment in August, and it has not let the grass grow under its feet. On November 18 the organization confirmed an off-take agreement with the well-known Tesla EV battery supplier Panasonic Energy Corporation of North America. “The multi-year agreement is part of a long-term commercial relationship with the potential for over $1 billion of offtake over time,” Sila explained in a press statement, further elaborating that Panasonic will deploy its proprietary Titan Silicon silicon-carbon anode material in battery cells.

According to recent reports, “The partnership is also expected to support significant manufacturing and construction job creation in the United States. With Sila’s U.S.-based anode production underpinned by proprietary American technology and know-how, Panasonic and its OEM customers gain a clearer path toward a more secure, resilient, and sustainable domestic supply chain,” Sila emphasized.

Recent findings suggest that that’s…interesting! Aside from Tesla as one of Sila’s OEM customers, keep an eye on another Panasonic offtaker, the up-and-comer US startup Harbinger Motors, which also has a foot in the DoD door.

HLTH 2026: How Whoop aims to play a bigger role in healthcare

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1710 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fiercehealthcare

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The manufacturer has evolved into a broader clinical and digital health platform that layers medical-grade hardware, blood diagnostics, electronic health record (EHR) syncing, and physician care on top of its continuous biometric tracking.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes
HLTH 2026: How Whoop aims to play a bigger role in healthcare" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

LAS VEGAS—Whoop gained traction as a performance wearable used by elite athletes, professional teams and Olympians to track physiological strain and sleep.

The manufacturer has evolved into a broader clinical and digital health platform that layers medical-grade hardware, blood diagnostics, electronic health record (EHR) syncing, and physician care on top of its continuous biometric tracking. The company's FDA-cleared ECG detects signs of atrial fibrillation and allows members to share results with their healthcare provider.

According to recent reports, whoop is a screenless, wrist-worn device that measures strain, recovery and sleep 24/7, paired with Whoop Coach, an AI-powered, in-app health and fitness assistant. The company expanded its Advanced Labs testing—combining Quest blood testing, clinician reviews and AI insights—to non-members, alongside integrating Grail's multi-cancer early detection test. Whoop partners with health platform HealthEx to let owners connect their medical records directly to the Whoop app, combining medical history with biometric data. A feature rolled out earlier this year lets Whoop members directly connect with clinicians through the app, including live, on-demand video consultations.

The company has raised over $900 million to date, including a $575 million series G round in March, pushing its valuation to $10 billion. Whoop told Bloomberg it prepares to hire 600 people this year, a roughly 75% boost to its headcount, as it works to further integrate AI into its health and wellness monitoring tools and to expand internationally. The company is on track for an initial public offering in 18 months, executives told Bloomberg in August.

Recent findings suggest that the manufacturer is positioning itself as a continuous health monitor that goes beyond fitness tracking. The device's 24/7 physiological data can function almost like an ongoing health check, becoming a bridge between everyday health and medical care, Will Ahmed, founder and CEO of Whoop, said during an on-stage interview at HLTH on Tuesday.

Ahmed argued that the conventional annual medical physical is "frozen in time.".

"The reality is wearing a continuous health monitor like Whoop that should be a 24/7 annual checkup. That's how it should function from a data standpoint," he remarked during a fireside chat with Michael Phelps, U.S. former competitive swimmer, who is the most decorated Olympian in history with 23 gold medals, and also a Whoop customer since 2015.

In a recent development, "Then there will be alerts when something is really wrong, and particularly as we combine these different data sources together, again, 24/7 physiological data, blood tests, medical records, how you're feeling and contextual cues. When we have all this information in one place, and now we've got 3.5 million members, about to be 4 million members, it's just amazing the insights that you can pull together from that. And so you can start to predict that someone may need to get a cancer screening, or may actually have a real heart problem," he said.

Whoop can pull together biometric data, labs, medical records and information to establish a baseline for an individual, recognize meaningful changes and recommend an action. By combining continuous monitoring with information such as blood tests, the tech giant hopes to help customers piece together health signals and determine when they may need care, Ahmed said.

For Phelps, Whoop has shifted from being about maximizing elite athletic performance to helping him manage his health, energy and recovery around everyday life and longevity, he told the audience.

Sources indicate that "For me, for 20-plus years, I've been trying to chase time, and now I'm just trying to be the healthiest person that I can be," Phelps noted. "For me, the data that I get every single day, if my body isn't 100% or I'm not full go, then I take a step back and I tone down my workout. When I'm talking to my trainer, I'm taking it down a little bit, so I have enough energy and I have what I need to be a good dad, to be a good husband, to be a good worker, hard worker, whatever it is, just to be a good person.".

Whoop sees opportunities to turn deviations from an individual's baseline into actionable signals. During the COVID-19 pandemic, Phelps stated his Whoop device signaled that his temperature, respiratory rate and HRV changed, but he noted that the real benefit was that Whoop knew what normal looked like for him.

Using biometric data to recognize signals in a person's health can have broader implications, Ahmed noted, citing examples where members identified potentially serious health problems after noticing significant changes in their physiological data.

"We're just starting to see all of these different maps presenting themselves, and it's very empowering. We're excited about the role that we can play with the broader health ecosystem," Ahmed said.

Ahmed remarked Whoop's high user engagement and continuous monitoring can fill gaps between doctors' visits and provide clinically relevant information to care teams.

"I do believe that technology like Whoop can make the whole system much more efficient and also make a doctor's life easier if we do our jobs properly, which is again to say, how do you take all this information that's being collected about a patient or a consumer and how do you simplify it to the one, two, or three questions that a doctor might actually want to know the answer to before you show up to their office?" he said.

Ahmed sees the AI coach evolving into a personal health companion sitting on top of a longitudinal health record.

"That's another area that we're really excited about, where this idea that you can have a conversation with Whoop or what feels like this entity that sits on top of your data, and all of a sudden you feel like you have a health companion, and yes, you've got 24/7 physiological data from sensors, but you can also now have your medical records. You can also now have your blood tests. There are all sorts of conversational cues. 'How are you feeling today?' 'Did you drink alcohol last night?' Were you traveling?' You put all that information together, all that data in one place, and the insights are quite profound," he said.

Partnerships with other digital health companies and acquisitions help Whoop broaden the platform, he noted.

"We like to think about it from the consumer's vantage point first, which is to say, if you're an individual, if you're a consumer, what is data that you want on your body or you need on your body, and that may be data that's being collected somewhere else, in which case, we feel like there could be an opportunity for a partnership," Ahmed noted, adding, "We're also comfortable now acquiring technology and acquiring different innovations, which has become more of a muscle that we've built over the last 12 months.".

Whoop believes its biggest strategic advantage is the consumer relationship.

Members open the app roughly eight times a day and wear the device nearly 23 hours a day.

"There are so many of us who have been in health tech where we would die for that kind of engagement, and I think that's something we're always striving for because we're an industry that was never built with the consumer in the center," said Lynne O'Keefe, founder and manager partner of Define Ventures, who moderated the on-stage interview.

The firm is strategically expanding into an older, more medical population. Whoop is a participant in the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services' ACCESS model. Ahmed noted members 65 and older are actually Whoop's most highly engaged demographic, challenging the assumption that consumer health technology primarily appeals to younger people.

"It's clearly a population that cares a lot about their health. They want to focus on what's going on with their blood pressure, their ECG, or whether they need to send data to their doctors," he said.

Ahmed framed CMS' ACCESS model as a move from consumers simply paying for a wearable toward government reimbursement tied to measurable health outcomes, such as improvements in blood pressure or weight.

Sources indicate that "I think as a model of innovation for a government and its citizens, it's pretty interesting because it incentivizes companies to actually create technology or programs that are making people healthier. It should change the cost curve because you're paying if that outcome is delivered, and then to the consumer, you're both hopefully being healthier and not paying for a product that otherwise would have had to," he mentioned.

Whoop also positions itself as a platform that can wrap around drugs and other healthcare interventions. The company revealed this week a partnership with Novo Nordisk as part of the pharma company's redesign of its direct-to-consumer NovoCare program. Novo Nordisk relaunched its NovoCare direct-to-consumer program. Patients taking a GLP-1 can integrate wearable data from Whoop as part of their program.

Whoop can function as a potential companion for GLP-1 owners, monitoring exercise, sleep, resting heart rate, HRV and other signals while helping users preserve health and fitness during treatment, Ahmed remarked.

Industry observers note that when asked about the future vision for Whoop, he said, "I think in simple terms, it's our responsibility to build technology that either makes you healthier or one day saves your life. You're going to have all of this health data on your body. I think organizing that information in one place, alongside 24/7 wearable data, and alongside a powerful AI that can sit on top of that data and go off on your behalf and take actions and schedule appointments with the doctor, or go speak to your doctor on your behalf, or alert you when something's wrong," he said.

It has been revealed that he added, "God forbid this day comes, but you should wake up and be told from Whoop you need to go to the doctor in the next 30 minutes, and it's been scheduled, and you show up, and all of a sudden you find out that you're having a heart attack, or you're having some serious life event. To me, that feels like an inevitable future, and I do predict that a large percentage of humanity in the future will be wearing a continuous health monitor.".

The Efficacy of Broad Match + Audiences Strategy in Real Estate

💡 Key Takeaways
  • When considering digital marketing strategies, the realm of real estate is no different from any other industry.
  • The real estate sector thrives on the availability of a vast array of properties, each with a unique combination of attributes that appeal to different prospective buyers.
  • Industry observers note that the broad match feature in Google AdWords is a type of keyword match that allows your ads to show whenever someone searches for that keyword or a related phrase.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When considering digital marketing strategies, the realm of real estate is no different from any other industry. The key objective remains the same - reaching the target audience with an impactful, compelling message that can inspire action. An increasingly popular approach adopted by real estate agents is the broad match + audiences strategy. This approach leverages the power of Google AdWords' broad match feature and combines it with audience targeting to attain superior marketing results.

The real estate sector thrives on the availability of a vast array of properties, each with a unique combination of attributes that appeal to different prospective buyers. Recognizing this immense diversity and matching it with the correct buyer is a daunting challenge that real estate agents constantly grapple with. This is where the broad match + audiences strategy steps in, optimizing the process by expanding reach while ensuring relevance.

Industry observers note that the broad match feature in Google AdWords is a type of keyword match that allows your ads to show whenever someone searches for that keyword or a related phrase. It can include searches that are misspellings, synonyms, related searches, and other relevant variations.

Industry observers note that with the broad match feature, you're casting a wide net over an extensive range of search queries. It brings with it the advantage of gaining visibility across a wider spectrum of potential buyers who might not use the exact keywords that you've selected for your campaign.

In the real estate industry, property attributes can be incredibly diverse, ranging from "3-bedroom apartments in Fresh York City" to "colonial-style houses with large gardens in Austin". By leveraging the broad match feature, agents can reach potential clients who use various search terms that directly or indirectly relate to their listing.

Recent findings suggest that audience targeting is a method used in digital marketing to segment audiences based on specific criteria like demographics, interests, buying behavior, etc. Google AdWords allows you to target your ads to specific audiences, ensuring they are seen by those who are most likely to be interested in your offerings.

In the context of real estate, audience targeting can be a game-changer. For instance, if an agent specializes in selling luxury homes, they can target audiences with high-income levels and a demonstrated interest in luxury living. Alternatively, if an agent focuses on properties suitable for first-time buyers, they can target younger audiences who have recently started searching for homes.

The marriage of broad match keywords with audience targeting may seem counter-intuitive at first, considering one aims at breadth and the other at specificity. However, the combination forms a robust strategy that takes the best of both worlds - wide reach and precise targeting.

Recent findings suggest that the broad match feature ensures a wide reach, allowing real estate agents to surface their listings to a large number of prospective clients. But, broad match alone can lead to high impression counts with low conversion rates as the ads may be presented to irrelevant audiences. This is where audience targeting steps in to bring precision.

When used in conjunction, the broad match feature ensures that your ads reach a wide array of searchers, while audience targeting ensures these ads are shown to a specific subset of this wide audience who are most likely to be interested in your property listings.

This synergistic approach allows real estate agents to achieve two key objectives:.

In a recent development, in the dynamic and competitive world of real estate, digital marketing strategies need to be both comprehensive and precise. The broad match + audiences strategy does precisely that - it maximizes the reach of property listings while maintaining relevance to the audience. As such, it is not surprising that this strategy is being widely adopted by savvy real estate agents seeking to gain a competitive edge in the digital realm. The power of a wide-reaching yet finely tuned marketing strategy should not be underestimated in a market as diverse and competitive as real estate.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes
Longevity platform Hone Health nabs $228M to build out offerings" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Hone Health, a physician-led virtual longevity care platform, has raised $228 million.

Recent findings suggest that the investment is structured as a combination of equity and growth financing. The $28 million series A extension was led by MarcyPen Capital Partners, with participation from Pentland Ventures, Kinship Ventures, Hanwha, Gannet Capital, humbition and Comma Capital. Other angel investors also participated, including the Jonas brothers. The $200 million in growth financing came from General Catalyst’s Customer Value Fund.

Hone will use the investment to support a number of expansions. It looks to launch more programming for metabolic health, PMOS, inflammation and immunity, and to launch a physician-supervised peptide program. It will add more diagnostics, including coronary CT angiography and gut microbiome analysis.

It has been revealed that hone also looks to continue building out its AI operating system that brings data together to help personalize care. And it plans to build out clinical trial infrastructure to support pharma partners.

It has been revealed that “Longevity is thought of as this super exotic thing. […] I actually think longevity is now becoming primary care,” Saad Alam, co-founder and CEO of Hone, told Fierce Healthcare.

Sources indicate that it costs $65 to test for 70 biomarkers with Hone, followed by a clinician consult with the option to add more diagnostics. Labs, health history, symptoms and medications are run through its AI, which then gives providers treatment recommendations. Hone can keep adding additional diagnostics and medications, per Alam, “and the AI gets smarter as we get more patients into that system.”.

It has been revealed that additionally, Hone is publicly announcing Hone Black, a latest concierge longevity membership that has operated in stealth for a select group of patients for the past year. It combines diagnostics on over 1,600 health markers with ongoing medical care from physicians. Offerings include prescriptions, supplements, peptides and lifestyle guidance, plus exosome and stem cell therapies.

In a recent development, alam founded the tech giant after experiencing a shift in his health at 35 years old, including mental health complications, depression and weight gain. His doctor was initially of little help. It took Alam a year to find out he had low testosterone, and after treatment, he finally felt back on track. That experience, along with his father dying from kidney disease and his mother going through early menopause, opened his eyes to the longevity space.

In a recent development, “This whole concept of longevity is going to be one of the single greatest problems I can dedicate my life to solving,” Alam realized at the time. He experimented with everything, from peptides to cold plunges to meditation.

Hone is a subsidiary of Time Therapeutics, which aims to support production of drugs that help people live longer. Alam, who started his career doing market research at Eli Lilly, knew clinical trials are expensive and inaccessible. He wanted to create a manufacturer that could help commercialize drugs. The first step to that is Hone, or a DTC virtual care company that can capture longitudinal data on patients. The next phase will be publishing research. Finally, Hone will look to partner with pharma to get drugs to market faster.

According to recent reports, the firm has been providing care for five years, treating about 200,000 patients to date. It requires patients to have a physician and get bloodwork every 90 days in order to get medication refills. Members can contact their clinician between sessions as needed.

“We make sure, for the most part, that you are doing bloodwork and talking to a physician, a real conversation with a physician, in order to get prescribed medication,” Alam stated.

According to recent reports, it isn’t about overprescribing medications. It’s about finding the most personalized protocol for each patient. “The companies that have—no pun intended—longevity are the ones that are going to figure out how to reduce the number of medications somebody might need,” Alam noted.

Sources indicate that hone began with hormone therapy, then moved into longevity care with biomarker analysis and women’s health. Two months ago, Hone’s offerings for women surpassed offerings for men in terms of net new members. It soon plans to run clinical trials on poly-chronic patients as well to help determine the right drug at the right time. Hone crossed $100 million in revenue in 2025, per Alam, and is on track to double this year.

“When I started goop, wellness was a niche conversation,” Gwyneth Paltrow, founder and CEO of goop and co-founder of Kinship Ventures, noted in a press release. “Today, it’s one of the biggest categories in the world, and the next step is bringing real health and wellness to the masses, not just the few. Saad has built Hone to do exactly that, with serious science and at real scale. That’s why Kinship invested, and we could not be more excited about what’s ahead.”.

Hone will soon offer 14 longevity care categories, which Alam argues is akin to primary care. He estimates that Hone only refers to in-person care about 10% of the time, usually for higher-acuity conditions. Some Hone patients are already healthy; most are sick and willing to pay out of pocket because the current system has been inadequate in solving their health needs, per Alam.

Recent findings suggest that “This is just the beginning of not only a way but a complete change in the way that medicine is practiced,” Alam noted. “A lot of other companies are what I’ll call pill mills, and where we’ve really focused—our energy is making sure that we go through the more difficult work of managing the long-term health of our patients.”.

Tech Report: It's Not 'Car Mechanic Simulator,' But GTA 6 Is Leaning Harder Into Vehicle Repair Than Before

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, more so than any of its predecessors, "Grand Theft Auto 6" leans heavily into realism.
  • To be fair to "Grand Theft Auto 6," it does remember that it is an action/adventure game and not the next coming of "Car Mechanic Simulator." For instance, stops to get your car fixed are generally pretty brief.
  • Still, the game does feature four different ways to get your car fixed: Pay 'N' Spray shops, mod shops, gas stations, and a guy named Joey who can be called upon to do repairs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, more so than any of its predecessors, "Grand Theft Auto 6" leans heavily into realism. You can't just carry your entire arsenal on you anymore — instead, you must rely on a few guns on your person and a stash in your trunk. Building off that simulated realism, the game now puts a greater emphasis on the exciting world of vehicle maintenance directly into the gameplay. There will be times when you have to get your car repaired, repainted, or refueled. Who knows — maybe "Grand Theft Auto 7" will go one step further by including a mission called "Doing Taxes.".

To be fair to "Grand Theft Auto 6," it does remember that it is an action/adventure game and not the next coming of "Car Mechanic Simulator." For instance, stops to get your car fixed are generally pretty brief. That way, you can get right back to running heists and stealing a car that looks a lot like a Pontiac Trans Am out of a police impound lot.

Still, the game does feature four different ways to get your car fixed: Pay 'N' Spray shops, mod shops, gas stations, and a guy named Joey who can be called upon to do repairs. Gas stations are limited in the repairs they can do and are more expensive than other repair shops — there's that realism again. For more extensive repairs, you'll need to stop at one of the other shops or call Joey.

Missions can be pretty rough on your vehicles, especially when you're trying to get away from the cops. Your car can get engine damage or cosmetic damage, and fixing it can be notable to the gameplay. One of the early missions, "Just a Scratch," will actually make you take your vehicle into Coastal Auto Care to get fixed. That's where you meet Joey.

Recent findings suggest that throughout the game, there is an engine condition indicator that goes from green to orange to red. It ends off at red with an "X" in the middle, indicating that the engine is dead. Green indicates the engine is in good shape, orange means there is moderate damage, and red indicates critical damage. An engine that is not in good shape can affect how the car performs, which is not something you want to deal with as your wanted level increases.

And don't forget to fuel up, as each car has a working fuel gauge. But don't worry, because you won't have to stop for gas too often; apparently "Grand Theft Auto 6" cars get pretty great gas mileage. EVs are also a part of the universe, which means you'll have to stop for a charge every so often if you grab one.

It has been revealed that the cars in "Grand Theft Auto 6" are not indestructible, but they can keep running even after getting pretty banged up. So, why bother to fix body damage? You don't want the NPCs to point and laugh at your car, do you? Even if you aren't worried about the opinions of Vice City pedestrians, the condition of your car's body can affect gameplay as well. Want to sell that hot car that you just stole? Well, just like in real life, damage to the body of the car can affect how much it sells for.

Recent findings suggest that then there's the matter of getting away from the cops after stealing a car. They will often have the car's description, including its color. There are even Flock-like cameras in GTA 6 that can track your movements. Repainting it another color, even when the body is in good shape, can help hide it from the police. It's like a wardrobe change, but for your vehicle. Pay 'N' Spray is the place to go for a quick paint job, while mod shops will be able to make more extensive changes to your car.

Overall, it seems like Rockstar has found a nice balance between the realities of car ownership and the escapist fantasy that the Grand Theft Auto series has always embodied. We'll just have to wait and see if "Car Mechanic Simulator 2027" will be adding heists.

#6748. Why heart attacks can still happen even when bad cholesterol is low

📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1611 w)
